(d) every assessor or member of a panchayat assisting a Court or public servant; 
(e) every arbitrator or other person to whom any cause or matter has been referred for 
decision or report by any Court, or by any other competent public authority; 
(f) every person who holds any office by virtue of which he is empowered to place or 
keep any person in confinement; 
(g) every officer of the Government whose duty it is, as such officer, to prevent offences, 
to give information of offences, to bring offenders to justice, or to protect the public health, 
safety or convenience; 
(h) every officer whose duty it is, as such officer, to take, receive, keep or expend any 
property on behalf of the Government, or to make any survey, assessment or contract on 
behalf of the Government, or to execute any revenue-process, or to investigate, or to report, 
on any matter affecting the pecuniary interests of the Government, or to make, authenticate 
or keep any document relating to the pecuniary interests of the Government, or to prevent the 
infraction of any law for the protection of the pecuniary interests of the Government; 
(i) every officer whose duty it is, as such officer, to take, receive, keep or expend any 
property, to make any survey or assessment or to levy any rate or tax for any secular common 
purpose of any village, town or district, or to make, authenticate or keep any document for 
the ascertaining of the rights of the people of any village, town or district; 
(j) every person who holds any office by virtue of which he is empowered to prepare, 
publish, maintain or revise an electoral roll or to conduct an election or part of an election; 
(k) every person— 
(i) in the service or pay of the Government or remunerated by fees or commission for 
the performance of any public duty by the Government; 
(ii) in the service or pay of a local authority as defined in clause (31) of section 3 of 
the General Clauses Act, 1897 (10 of 1897), a corporation established by or under a 
Central or State Act or a Government company as defined in clause (45) of section 2 of 
the Companies Act, 2013 (18 of 2013). 
Explanation.— 
(a) persons falling under any of the descriptions made in this clause are public servants, 
whether appointed by the Government or not; 
(b) every person who is in actual possession of the situation of a public servant, whatever 
legal defect there may be in his right to hold that situation is a public servant; 
(c) “election” means an election for the purpose of selecting members of any legislative, 
municipal or other public authority, of whatever character, the method of selection to which 
is by, or under any law for the time being in force. 
 A Municipal Commissioner is a public servant; 
(29) “reason to believe”.—A person is said to have “reason to believe” a thing, if he has 
sufficient cause to believe that thing but not otherwise; 
(30) “special law” means a law applicable to a particular subject; 
(31) “valuable security” means a document which is, or purports to be, a document whereby any 
legal right is created, extended, transferred, restricted, extinguished or released, or whereby any 
person acknowledges that he lies under legal liability, or has not a certain legal right.

(4) In every Part of this Sanhita, except where a contrary intention appears from the context, words 
which refer to acts done extend also to illegal omissions. 
(5) When a criminal act is done by several persons in furtherance of the common intention of all, 
each of such persons is liable for that act in the same manner as if it were done by him alone. 
(6) Whenever an act, which is criminal only by reason of its being done with a criminal knowledge or 
intention, is done by several persons, each of such persons who joins in the act with such knowledge or 
intention is liable for the act in the same manner as if the act were done by him alone with that knowledge 
or intention. 
(7) Wherever the causing of a certain effect, or an attempt to cause that effect, by an act or by an 
omission, is an offence, it is to be understood that the causing of that effect partly by an act and partly by 
an omission is the same offence. 
A intentionally causes Z’s death, partly by illegally omitting to give Z food, and partly by beating Z. 
A has committed murder. 
(8) When an offence is committed by means of several acts, whoever intentionally cooperates in the 
commission of that offence by doing any one of those acts, either singly or jointly with any other person, 
commits that offence. 
(a) A and B agree to murder Z by severally and at different times giving him small doses of poison. 
A and B administer the poison according to the agreement with intent to murder Z. Z dies from the 
effects the several doses of poison so administered to him. Here A and B intentionally cooperate in the 
commission of murder and as each of them does an act by which the death is caused, they are both guilty 
of the offence though their acts are separate. 
(b) A and B are joint jailors, and as such have the charge of Z, a prisoner, alternatively for six hours 
at a time. A and B, intending to cause Z’s death, knowingly cooperate in causing that effect by illegally 
omitting, each during the time of his attendance, to furnish Z with food supplied to them for that purpose. 
Z dies of hunger. Both A and B are guilty of the murder of Z. 
(c) A, a jailor, has the charge of Z, a prisoner. A, intending to cause Z’s death, illegally omits to 
supply Z with food; in consequence of which Z is much reduced in strength, but the starvation is not 
sufficient to cause his death. A is dismissed from his office, and B succeeds him. B, without collusion or 
cooperation with A, illegally omits to supply Z with food, knowing that he is likely thereby to cause Z’s 
death. Z dies of hunger. B is guilty of murder, but, as A did not cooperate with B. A is guilty only of an 
attempt to commit murder. 
(9) Where several persons are engaged or concerned in the commission of a criminal act, they may be 
guilty of different offences by means of that act.

to his own use any movable property, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a

(a) A takes property belonging to Z out of Z’s possession, in good faith believing at the time when he

(b) A, being on friendly terms with Z, goes into Z’s library in Z’s absence, and takes away a book 
without Z’s express consent. Here, if A was under the impression that he had Z’s implied consent to take 
the book for the purpose of reading it, A has not committed theft. But, if A afterwards sells the book for 
his own benefit, he is guilty of an offence under this section. 
(c) A and B, being, joint owners of a horse. A takes the horse out of B’s possession, intending to use 
it. Here, as A has a right to use the horse, he does not dishonestly misappropriate it. But, if A sells the

## Summary

A person was singing obscene songs and making vulgar gestures in a public park in front of women and children. Petition for relief is sought under Article 294 of BNS_2023 (public nuisance by doing any act which any class of persons, grieving thereby, may have a right to prevent), Article 294A (singing, reciting or uttering any obscene song, ballad or words, in or near any public place), and Article 39 of Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023 (protection of women and children).

## Applicable BNS provisions

* [BNS Section 296]
* [BNS Section 292]

## Recommendation / next steps

The accused should be tried for public nuisance under [BNS Section 296] and [BNS Section 292]. Given the presence of women and children in the public park, the court should also consider initiating proceedings under Article 39 of Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023 to ensure their safety and security. ## Summary
The user's ex-boyfriend has shared her private photographs on social media and created a fake profile using her pictures. He is accused of violating Article 377(2) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) for disclosure of private images and Article 479(1) for creating a false online profile using another person's image. The user seeks guidance under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) on filing a First Information Report (FIR), serving a notice to the accused, and the admissibility of digital evidence.

## Applicable BNS provisions

* [BNS Section 212]
* [BNS Section 336]
* [BNS Section 209]
* [BNS Section 353]
* [BNS Section 232]

## Recommendation / next steps
Given the circumstances, it appears that the user's ex-boyfriend has committed an offence under [BNS Section 212] by furnishing false information, which is likely to cause injury or annoyance to the user. He also appears to have committed forgery under [BNS Section 336] by creating a false document or electronic record, with intent to cause damage or injury to the user. 

To proceed, the user can file a complaint under [BNS Section 209] for non-appearance in response to a proclamation, as the accused may have failed to appear at the specified place and time as required by a proclamation. The user can also serve a notice to the accused under [BNS Section 353] for making a statement conducing to public mischief, with intent to cause fear or alarm to the public. 

The admissibility of digital evidence, such as screenshots of the social media posts and online profiles, can be considered under [BNS Section 336]. The burden of proof and presumptions in this matter can be clarified under [BNS Section 232] regarding threatening any person to give false evidence.

commission of that offence by doing any one of those acts, either singly or jointly with any other person, 
commits that offence. 
(a) A and B agree to murder Z by severally and at different times giving him small doses of poison. 
A and B administer the poison according to the agreement with intent to murder Z. Z dies from the 
effects the several doses of poison so administered to him. Here A and B intentionally cooperate in the 
commission of murder and as each of them does an act by which the death is caused, they are both guilty 
of the offence though their acts are separate. 
(b) A and B are joint jailors, and as such have the charge of Z, a prisoner, alternatively for six hours 
at a time. A and B, intending to cause Z’s death, knowingly cooperate in causing that effect by illegally 
omitting, each during the time of his attendance, to furnish Z with food supplied to them for that purpose. 
Z dies of hunger. Both A and B are guilty of the murder of Z. 
(c) A, a jailor, has the charge of Z, a prisoner. A, intending to cause Z’s death, illegally omits to 
supply Z with food; in consequence of which Z is much reduced in strength, but the starvation is not 
sufficient to cause his death. A is dismissed from his office, and B succeeds him. B, without collusion or 
cooperation with A, illegally omits to supply Z with food, knowing that he is likely thereby to cause Z’s 
death. Z dies of hunger. B is guilty of murder, but, as A did not cooperate with B. A is guilty only of an 
attempt to commit murder. 
(9) Where several persons are engaged or concerned in the commission of a criminal act, they may be 
guilty of different offences by means of that act.

culpable homicide not amounting to murder. B, having ill-will towards Z and intending to kill him, and 
not having been subject to the provocation, assists A in killing Z. Here, though A and B are both engaged 
in causing Z’s death, B is guilty of murder, and A is guilty only of culpable homicide.

information to be false, and knowing that it is likely that the consequence of the information will be a

(c) A falsely informs a policeman that he has been assaulted and robbed in the neighbourhood of

Punishment for false evidence.—(1) Whoever intentionally gives false evidence in any stage 
of a judicial proceeding, or fabricates false evidence for the purpose of being used in any stage of a 
judicial proceeding, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may 
extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine which may extend to ten thousand rupees. 
(2) Whoever intentionally gives or fabricates false evidence in any case other than that referred to in

Explanation 1.—A trial before a Court-martial is a judicial proceeding. 
Explanation 2.—An investigation directed by law preliminary to a proceeding before a Court, is a 
stage of a judicial proceeding, though that investigation may not take place before a Court. 
A, in an enquiry before a Magistrate for the purpose of ascertaining whether Z ought to be committed 
for trial, makes on oath a statement which he knows to be false. As this enquiry is a stage of a judicial 
proceeding, A has given false evidence.

Explanation 3.—An investigation directed by a Court according to law, and conducted under the 
authority of a Court, is a stage of a judicial proceeding, though that investigation may not take place 
before a Court. 

A, in an enquiry before an officer deputed by a Court to ascertain on the spot the boundaries of land, 
makes on oath a statement which he knows to be false. As this enquiry is a stage of a judicial proceeding, 
A has given false evidence.

Threatening any person to give false evidence.—(1) Whoever threatens another with any 
injury to his person, reputation or property or to the person or reputation of any one in whom that person 
is interested, with intent to cause that person to give false evidence shall be punished with imprisonment 
of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, or with fine, or with both. 
(2) If innocent person is convicted and sentenced in consequence of false evidence referred to in 
sub-section (1), with death or imprisonment for more than seven years, the person who threatens shall be

Pursuant to the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023, whether the sale of obscene materials (as defined under Article 12 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023) to minor school children (as per Article 5 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023) near a school campus amounts to an offence under Article 3 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023, specifically with regards to the protection of minors and the preservation of public decency.

Further, under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023, what legal action can be taken by the authorities to prohibit and penalize such activities, and what procedural safeguards are available to ensure the protection of the rights of the affected minors under Section 11 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023?
result.answer:
## Summary
The sale of obscene materials to minor school children near a school campus may amount to an offence under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 (BNS_2023). The sale of obscene materials to children is specifically prohibited under BNS Section 295, which prescribes punishment for selling, letting to hire, distributing, exhibiting, or circulating obscene objects to children.

## Applicable BNS provisions
- [BNS Section 295]
- [BNS Section 294]

## Recommendation / next steps
The authorities should take immediate action to prohibit and penalize the sale of obscene materials to minor school children near the school campus. Under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023, the police can issue a proclamation under Section 84, declaring the person responsible for the sale of obscene materials as a proclaimed offender. If the person fails to appear in response to the proclamation, they may be punished under BNS Section 209. The authorities should also consider filing a complaint under BNS Section 292 for public nuisance, as the sale of obscene materials to children may be considered a public nuisance.

Now, it is proposed to enact a new law, namely, the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita Bill, 2023 by 
repealing the Indian Penal Code to streamline provisions relating to offences and penalties. It is proposed

Now, it is proposed to enact a new law, namely, the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita Bill, 2023 by 
repealing the Indian Penal Code to streamline provisions relating to offences and penalties. It is proposed 
to provide first time community service as one of the punishments for petty offences. The offences 
against women and children, murder and offences against the State have been given precedence. The 
various offences have been made gender neutral. In order to deal effectively with the problem of 
organised crimes and terrorist activities, new offences of terrorist acts and organised crime have been 
added in the Bill with deterrent punishments. A new offence on acts of secession, armed rebellion, 
subversive activities, separatist activities or endangering sovereignty or unity and integrity of India has 
also been added. The fines and punishment for various offences have also been suitably enhanced.

or intention.

omission, is an offence, it is to be understood that the causing of that effect partly by an act and partly by

commission of that offence by doing any one of those acts, either singly or jointly with any other person,

A and B administer the poison according to the agreement with intent to murder Z. Z dies from the 
effects the several doses of poison so administered to him. Here A and B intentionally cooperate in the 
commission of murder and as each of them does an act by which the death is caused, they are both guilty 
of the offence though their acts are separate.

at a time. A and B, intending to cause Z’s death, knowingly cooperate in causing that effect by illegally 
omitting, each during the time of his attendance, to furnish Z with food supplied to them for that purpose.

supply Z with food; in consequence of which Z is much reduced in strength, but the starvation is not 
sufficient to cause his death. A is dismissed from his office, and B succeeds him. B, without collusion or 
cooperation with A, illegally omits to supply Z with food, knowing that he is likely thereby to cause Z’s 
death. Z dies of hunger. B is guilty of murder, but, as A did not cooperate with B. A is guilty only of an 
attempt to commit murder.

Petition for Redressal: 
 Whether the actions of a person, as described, constituting the deliberate display of obscene visual content to unsuspecting individuals, particularly women, on a public thoroughfare, amounts to an offence under Article 321, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 (BNS), and if so, whether the provisions of Article 123, BNS, are applicable in this instance.

Further, whether the circumstances of this case warrant the issuance of a summons under Article 21, Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023 (BNSS), and whether the same may be served upon the aforementioned individual, thereby commencing legal proceedings against him.

Additionally, whether the visual content displayed by the individual is admissible as evidence under Article 45, Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023 (BSA) and if so, whether the requirements of Article 34, BSA, regarding the authentication of digital evidence, have been satisfied in this case.

## Summary
The man is accused of deliberately displaying obscene images on his phone to unsuspecting women in a public place. This act may potentially fall under various provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS). The petitioner seeks to know if Article 321, BNS, is applicable, whether the provisions of Article 123, BNS, are relevant, and if a summons should be issued under Article 21, Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS). Additionally, the petitioner wants to know if the visual content displayed is admissible as evidence under Article 45, Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) and if the requirements of Article 34, BSA, regarding authentication of digital evidence, have been satisfied.

## Applicable BNS provisions
[BNS Section 294] 
[BNS Section 75]
[BNS Section 77]
[BNS Section 353]

## Recommendation / next steps
Based on the information provided, it appears that the man's actions may be considered an offence under the BNS. Article 294, BNS, deals with the sale, etc., of obscene objects, which could be applicable in this case as the man is displaying obscene images. Article 75, BNS, deals with sexual harassment, and the man's actions could be considered a form of sexual harassment. Article 77, BNS, deals with voyeurism, and the man's actions could be considered a form of voyeurism. Article 353, BNS, deals with statements conducing to public mischief, and the man's actions could be considered a form of public mischief.

Given the potential offences, it would be advisable to issue a summons under Article 21, BNSS, to the man, requiring him to appear before a court and face charges. The visual content displayed by the man may be admissible as evidence under Article 45, BSA, but the requirements of Article 34, BSA, regarding authentication of digital evidence, would need to be satisfied before it can be used as evidence.

(6) Whenever an act, which is criminal only by reason of its being done with a criminal knowledge or 
intention, is done by several persons, each of such persons who joins in the act with such knowledge or 
intention is liable for the act in the same manner as if the act were done by him alone with that knowledge 
or intention.

omission, is an offence, it is to be understood that the causing of that effect partly by an act and partly by

commission of that offence by doing any one of those acts, either singly or jointly with any other person,

effects the several doses of poison so administered to him. Here A and B intentionally cooperate in the 
commission of murder and as each of them does an act by which the death is caused, they are both guilty 
of the offence though their acts are separate.

at a time. A and B, intending to cause Z’s death, knowingly cooperate in causing that effect by illegally 
omitting, each during the time of his attendance, to furnish Z with food supplied to them for that purpose.

supply Z with food; in consequence of which Z is much reduced in strength, but the starvation is not

cooperation with A, illegally omits to supply Z with food, knowing that he is likely thereby to cause Z’s 
death. Z dies of hunger. B is guilty of murder, but, as A did not cooperate with B. A is guilty only of an 
attempt to commit murder.

## Summary
The actions of the perpetrator, who broke into the woman's house late at night when she was alone and raped her, amount to a serious crime under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 (BNS). The complainant can file an FIR under Section 3(1) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023 (BNSS). The admissibility of evidence under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023 (BSA) is also applicable in this case.

- [BNS Section 76]
- [BNS Section 1]
- [BNS Section 4]

The complainant should immediately file an FIR under Section 3(1) of the BNSS, which is available under [BNS Section 1] (BNS_2023_s1), which explains the application of the BNS provisions. The police should then collect and preserve physical evidence and the testimonial evidence of the complainant, in accordance with the provisions of the BSA. The perpetrator can be charged under [BNS Section 76], which deals with assault or use of criminal force to a woman with intent to disrobe. The provisions of [BNS Section 4] also apply to this case, as it deals with the repeal of the Indian Penal Code and the new provisions of the BNS.

which refer to acts done extend also to illegal omissions. 
(5) When a criminal act is done by several persons in furtherance of the common intention of all, 
each of such persons is liable for that act in the same manner as if it were done by him alone. 
(6) Whenever an act, which is criminal only by reason of its being done with a criminal knowledge or 
intention, is done by several persons, each of such persons who joins in the act with such knowledge or 
intention is liable for the act in the same manner as if the act were done by him alone with that knowledge 
or intention. 
(7) Wherever the causing of a certain effect, or an attempt to cause that effect, by an act or by an 
omission, is an offence, it is to be understood that the causing of that effect partly by an act and partly by 
an omission is the same offence. 
A intentionally causes Z’s death, partly by illegally omitting to give Z food, and partly by beating Z. 
A has committed murder. 
(8) When an offence is committed by means of several acts, whoever intentionally cooperates in the 
commission of that offence by doing any one of those acts, either singly or jointly with any other person, 
commits that offence. 
(a) A and B agree to murder Z by severally and at different times giving him small doses of poison. 
A and B administer the poison according to the agreement with intent to murder Z. Z dies from the 
effects the several doses of poison so administered to him. Here A and B intentionally cooperate in the 
commission of murder and as each of them does an act by which the death is caused, they are both guilty 
of the offence though their acts are separate. 
(b) A and B are joint jailors, and as such have the charge of Z, a prisoner, alternatively for six hours 
at a time. A and B, intending to cause Z’s death, knowingly cooperate in causing that effect by illegally 
omitting, each during the time of his attendance, to furnish Z with food supplied to them for that purpose. 
Z dies of hunger. Both A and B are guilty of the murder of Z. 
(c) A, a jailor, has the charge of Z, a prisoner. A, intending to cause Z’s death, illegally omits to 
supply Z with food; in consequence of which Z is much reduced in strength, but the starvation is not 
sufficient to cause his death. A is dismissed from his office, and B succeeds him. B, without collusion or 
cooperation with A, illegally omits to supply Z with food, knowing that he is likely thereby to cause Z’s 
death. Z dies of hunger. B is guilty of murder, but, as A did not cooperate with B. A is guilty only of an 
attempt to commit murder. 
(9) Where several persons are engaged or concerned in the commission of a criminal act, they may be 
guilty of different offences by means of that act. 
A attacks Z under such circumstances of grave provocation that his killing of Z would be only 
culpable homicide not amounting to murder. B, having ill-will towards Z and intending to kill him, and 
not having been subject to the provocation, assists A in killing Z. Here, though A and B are both engaged 
in causing Z’s death, B is guilty of murder, and A is guilty only of culpable homicide.

(5) Any person who is a member of an organisation which is involved in terrorist act, shall be

ordered.—Whenever any person convicted of or charged with an offence, being in lawful custody for 
that offence, escapes from such custody, or whenever a public servant, in the exercise of the lawful 
powers of such public servant, orders a certain person to be apprehended for an offence, whoever,

preventing him from being apprehended, shall be punished in the manner following, namely:—

Whether the conduct of the college professor constitutes an offence under Section 324 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 (BNS), specifically with regards to the elements of 'unlawful sexual conduct' and 'exploitation of authority' as defined in BNS.

Further, whether the provisions of Section 114(2) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023 (BNSS) are applicable in this scenario, considering the professor's abuse of authority and power to secure sexual favours from the student, thereby amounting to an 'offence against the dignity of a person' as per BNSS.

Additionally, under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023 (BSA), whether the testimony of the female student constitutes 'relevant evidence' under Section 60 of the BSA, considering the student's statement as a witness to the alleged offence committed by the professor.
result.answer:
## Summary

A college professor, being in a position of authority, has asked a female student for sexual favors in exchange for better grades. This conduct raises concerns under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 (BNS). The key issue is whether the professor's actions constitute an offense under BNS, particularly with regards to "unlawful sexual conduct" and "exploitation of authority." Additionally, the applicability of provisions from the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023 (BNSS) and the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023 (BSA) needs to be examined.

## Applicable BNS provisions

* [BNS Section 68] - Sexual intercourse by a person in authority
* [BNS Section 75] - Sexual harassment
* [BNS Section 76] - Assault or use of criminal force to woman with intent to disrobe
* [BNS Section 199] - Public servant disobeying direction under law
* [BNS Section 232] - Threatening any person to give false evidence

## Recommendation / next steps

Based on the above analysis, the professor's conduct may be considered an offense under BNS, specifically under Section 68 (Sexual intercourse by a person in authority), as he has abused his position to induce the student to have sexual intercourse. Additionally, his actions may also be seen as an offense of sexual harassment under Section 75.

Under Section 68, the professor may be liable for punishment, which includes rigorous imprisonment of either description for a term not less than five years, but which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.

Regarding the provisions of BNSS, specifically Section 114(2), it may be applicable in this scenario as the professor has abused his authority and power to secure sexual favors from the student, thereby amounting to an "offence against the dignity of a person."

Finally, under BSA, Section 60, the testimony of the female student would likely be considered "relevant evidence" in this case, as she is a witness to the alleged offense committed by the professor.

It is essential to note that the specific consequences and punishments would depend on the circumstances of the case and the discretion of the court.

Whether the actions of the accused, involving the intentional physical restraint and attempted removal of the victim's dupatta, amount to an offence under Article 226 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 (BNS), specifically in relation to the provisions governing outraging the modesty of a woman.

Furthermore, whether the conduct of the accused, committed in a public place and witnessed by others, constitutes a breach of Article 311 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023 (BNSS), specifically in relation to the provisions governing public order and decency.

Additionally, whether the statements of the witnesses who observed the incident can be admitted as evidence under Article 157(2) of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023 (BSA), specifically in relation to the provisions governing the admissibility of eyewitness testimony in cases of public decency violations.
result.answer:
## Summary

The accused's actions of grabbing the woman's dupatta and attempting to disrobe her in a public place, witnessed by others, may lead to multiple charges under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 (BNS). The incident involves intentional physical restraint and the attempt to remove the victim's clothing, which could be considered an assault or use of criminal force with intent to outrage her modesty. The conduct also breaches public order and decency provisions.

## Applicable BNS provisions

* [BNS Section 74] – Assault or use of criminal force to woman with intent to outrage her modesty.
* [BNS Section 76] – Assault or use of criminal force to woman with intent to disrobe.

## Recommendation / next steps

The accused should be investigated and charged under the relevant provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 (BNS). Specifically, the accused may be charged with:

- Assault or use of criminal force to woman with intent to outrage her modesty under Section 74, which carries a punishment of imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than one year but which may extend to five years, and a fine.
- Assault or use of criminal force to woman with intent to disrobe under Section 76, which carries a punishment of imprisonment of either description for a term which shall not be less than three years but which may extend to seven years, and a fine.

The court may consider other relevant provisions, such as those related to public order and decency, when determining the appropriate charges and penalties.

A married man had sexual intercourse with his wife during judicial separation against her will. We need to determine if this act constitutes an offense under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 (BNS) and what protection or recourse is available to the affected wife under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023 (BNSS) and Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023 (BSA).

## Applicable BNS provisions

* Section 67 - Sexual intercourse by husband upon his wife during separation.
* Section 85 - Husband or relative of husband of a woman subjecting her to cruelty.

Based on the given context, the act of the married man engaging in sexual intercourse with his wife during judicial separation against her will constitutes an offense under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 (BNS). Section 85 of the BNS provides for the punishment of cruelty by a husband or his relative against a wife, which may also be applicable in this case considering the wife's will was not taken into account.

However, it is essential to note that the specific circumstances of the case, such as the nature of the separation and the wife's consent status, would need to be considered during a thorough investigation and trial.

As for the protection or recourse available to the affected wife, it may involve filing a complaint under Section 67 or Section 85 of the BNS, depending on the specific circumstances of the case. Whether the act of installing the hidden camera and recording videos amounts to an offence under the aforesaid provisions and whether the accused can be held liable for the same, is a matter to be determined by the court, in accordance with the principles of law laid down in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023. result.answer:
## Summary
A man secretly installed a hidden camera in the women's changing room of a gym to record videos without the consent of the individuals whose private images were being captured. The complainant seeks to register a complaint under 'Unlawful Capture of Private Images' (Section 65 BNS). The court will determine whether the act of installing the hidden camera and recording videos amounts to an offence under BNS provisions.

## Applicable BNS provisions
[BNS Section 77], [BNS Section 59], [BNS Section 201], [BNS Section 212], [BNS Section 35], [BNS Section 303], [BNS Section 232], [BNS Section 34]

## Recommendation / next steps
Considering the provisions under BNS, the act of installing a hidden camera in the women's changing room and recording videos without consent falls under the category of 'Voyeurism' as per [BNS Section 77]. The perpetrator has committed an offence, which is punishable with imprisonment and fine.

The perpetrator, being a public servant, may have concealed his design or made false representations, which can attract punishment under [BNS Section 59] or [BNS Section 201] or [BNS Section 212].

Moreover, the perpetrator may have caused injury or annoyance to the victims, which can be considered under [BNS Section 232].

However, [BNS Section 34] provides that nothing is an offence which is done in the exercise of the right of private defence. Therefore, if the perpetrator can establish that his actions were done in private defence, it may be considered an exception.

The complainant can register a complaint under the category of 'Unlawful Capture of Private Images' (Section 65 BNS), and the court will determine the liability of the perpetrator based on the BNS provisions.

Petition for the imposition of Section 115(1) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 (BNS), namely, "Cheating by personation" and Section 498 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 (BNS) namely, "Husband or relative of husband of a woman subjecting her to cruelty", 

under Section 190 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023 (BNSS), namely, "Police officer's power to investigate cognizable cases", for an offense allegedly committed by the aforementioned man.

The pertinent facts of the case are as follows: 

- The man deceived the woman into believing they were lawfully married.
- He cohabited with her for several months.

It is prayed that the court may grant a direction to the police to register an FIR under the relevant provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 (BNS) and conduct a thorough investigation under the provisions of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023 (BNSS).

It is also prayed that the court may consider the admissibility of evidence under the provisions of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023 (BSA), particularly Section 32, namely, "Evidence of accomplices".

Additionally, it is prayed that the court may consider the applicability of Section 53 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023 (BSA) namely, "Collection of evidence by a police officer" to collect and preserve the evidence in this case.

Further, it is prayed that the court may consider the applicability of Section 165 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 (BNS) namely, "Sexual intercourse by a man with his own wife" if the parties are found to be 'lawfully married' after investigation.
result.answer:
## Summary

The man deceived a woman into believing they were lawfully married and cohabited with her for months. The petitioner is seeking the imposition of Section 115(1) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 (BNS) and Section 498 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 (BNS) under Section 190 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023 (BNSS), requesting the police to register an FIR and conduct a thorough investigation.

## Applicable BNS provisions

- [BNS Section 81] - Cohabitation caused by man deceitfully inducing belief of lawful marriage.
- [BNS Section 115(1)] - Cheating by personation.
- [BNS Section 498] - Husband or relative of husband of a woman subjecting her to cruelty.

## Recommendation / next steps

The court should direct the police to register an FIR under the relevant provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 (BNS) and conduct a thorough investigation under the provisions of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023 (BNSS). The admissibility of evidence under the provisions of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023 (BSA), particularly Section 32, should be considered for the accomplices' evidence. The collection and preservation of evidence should be done under the provisions of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023 (BSA), specifically Section 165.

Sanhita, 2023.

Official Gazette, appoint, and different dates may be appointed for different provisions of this Sanhita.

Pursuant to Article 498A of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 (BNS), the following legal query is posed:

Is the act of a person who is already in a subsisting marriage (as per Article 2, Clause (a) of the BNS) entering into a subsequent marriage with another woman without disclosing the existence of the prior marriage (in contravention of Article 2, Clause (c) of the BNS) cognizable under the provisions of the BNS?

Furthermore, under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023 (BNSS), is the said act punishable under the provisions of that Code, and if so, what are the appropriate measures that may be taken under Articles 123 and 124 of the BNSS to prevent and penalize this offense?

Additionally, in light of the circumstances, can the evidence of the second marriage be admitted as proof under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023 (BSA), and if so, what are the applicable rules of evidence that may be invoked to determine the admissibility and weight of such evidence?

## Summary
The man in question has committed a second marriage without disclosing his first marriage, which is a contravention of Article 2, Clause (c) of the BNS and [BNS Section 82]. Since he concealed the fact of the former marriage from the person with whom the subsequent marriage is contracted, he has committed an offence under [BNS Section 82]. The act of marrying again during the lifetime of a husband or wife, without proper disclosure, is punishable under the BNS.

## Applicable BNS provisions
- [BNS Section 82]
- [BNS Section 83]
- [BNS Section 81]

## Recommendation / next steps
The man in question can be tried and convicted for the offence committed under [BNS Section 82]. The appropriate measures that may be taken under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023 (BNSS) would be determined by the circumstances of the case. The evidence of the second marriage can be admitted as proof under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023 (BSA), and the applicable rules of evidence that may be invoked to determine the admissibility and weight of such evidence would depend on the specific circumstances of the case.

## Summary

The given scenario involves a woman leaving her newborn baby in a dustbin near the hospital and disappearing. Pursuant to the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 (BNS), the applicability of Section 317 (Abandonment of child under twelve years, by parent or person having care of it) to the facts of the case needs to be determined. (4) In every Part of this Sanhita, except where a contrary intention appears from the context, words 
which refer to acts done extend also to illegal omissions. 
(5) When a criminal act is done by several persons in furtherance of the common intention of all, 
each of such persons is liable for that act in the same manner as if it were done by him alone. 
(6) Whenever an act, which is criminal only by reason of its being done with a criminal knowledge or 
intention, is done by several persons, each of such persons who joins in the act with such knowledge or 
intention is liable for the act in the same manner as if the act were done by him alone with that knowledge 
or intention. 
(7) Wherever the causing of a certain effect, or an attempt to cause that effect, by an act or by an 
omission, is an offence, it is to be understood that the causing of that effect partly by an act and partly by 
an omission is the same offence. 
A intentionally causes Z’s death, partly by illegally omitting to give Z food, and partly by beating Z. 
A has committed murder. 
(8) When an offence is committed by means of several acts, whoever intentionally cooperates in the 
commission of that offence by doing any one of those acts, either singly or jointly with any other person, 
commits that offence. 
(a) A and B agree to murder Z by severally and at different times giving him small doses of poison. 
A and B administer the poison according to the agreement with intent to murder Z. Z dies from the 
effects the several doses of poison so administered to him. Here A and B intentionally cooperate in the 
commission of murder and as each of them does an act by which the death is caused, they are both guilty 
of the offence though their acts are separate. 
(b) A and B are joint jailors, and as such have the charge of Z, a prisoner, alternatively for six hours 
at a time. A and B, intending to cause Z’s death, knowingly cooperate in causing that effect by illegally 
omitting, each during the time of his attendance, to furnish Z with food supplied to them for that purpose. 
Z dies of hunger. Both A and B are guilty of the murder of Z. 
(c) A, a jailor, has the charge of Z, a prisoner. A, intending to cause Z’s death, illegally omits to 
supply Z with food; in consequence of which Z is much reduced in strength, but the starvation is not 
sufficient to cause his death. A is dismissed from his office, and B succeeds him. B, without collusion or 
cooperation with A, illegally omits to supply Z with food, knowing that he is likely thereby to cause Z’s 
death. Z dies of hunger. B is guilty of murder, but, as A did not cooperate with B. A is guilty only of an 
attempt to commit murder. 
(9) Where several persons are engaged or concerned in the commission of a criminal act, they may be 
guilty of different offences by means of that act. 
A attacks Z under such circumstances of grave provocation that his killing of Z would be only 
culpable homicide not amounting to murder. B, having ill-will towards Z and intending to kill him, and 
not having been subject to the provocation, assists A in killing Z. Here, though A and B are both engaged 
in causing Z’s death, B is guilty of murder, and A is guilty only of culpable homicide.

Pursuant to Article 265, Clause (a) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 (BNS), we seek clarification on the application of the provisions regarding the commission of "Offence of Exploitation of Vulnerable Person" (Section 45(5)) in relation to a scenario where a perpetrator, engaged in the organised activity of begging, has coerced minors aged 7-10 to solicit alms at traffic signals, thereby depriving them of their liberty and appropriating the proceeds of their labour. 

We would like to know whether the accused's actions constitute an offence under the said provision and, if so, what measures can be taken under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023 (BNSS) to ensure the safe recovery of the victims and subsequent prosecution of the perpetrator.

Furthermore, under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023 (BSA), we seek guidance on the admissibility of evidence obtained from the victims, including their testimonies and any corroborating documentary evidence, in establishing the facts of the case and securing a conviction.
result.answer:
## Summary
The scenario involves a begging ring operator who coerced minors aged 7-10 to beg at traffic signals and deprived them of their liberty by appropriating the proceeds of their labour. The perpetrator's actions constitute an offence under the provision related to the "Offence of Exploitation of Vulnerable Person" (Section 45(5)). The accused's use of minors for begging falls under the definition of trafficking, as they have been induced to perform work through the giving or receiving of payments or benefits.

## Applicable BNS provisions
[BNS Section 139], [BNS Section 45(5)]

## Recommendation / next steps
To ensure the safe recovery of the victims and subsequent prosecution of the perpetrator, the following measures can be taken under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023 (BNSS):

* The victims should be rescued and provided with necessary care and protection.
* The perpetrator should be apprehended and charged with the relevant offences under the BNSS.
* The victims' testimonies and any corroborating documentary evidence should be admissible in establishing the facts of the case and securing a conviction, as per the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023 (BSA).
* The perpetrator's actions should be investigated and prosecuted under the relevant provisions of the BNSS, including Section 139, which deals with kidnapping or maiming a child for purposes of begging.

effects the several doses of poison so administered to him. Here A and B intentionally cooperate in the 
commission of murder and as each of them does an act by which the death is caused, they are both guilty 
of the offence though their acts are separate.

the Court, and every person specially authorised by a Court to perform any of such duties; 
(d) every assessor or member of a panchayat assisting a Court or public servant; 
(e) every arbitrator or other person to whom any cause or matter has been referred for 
decision or report by any Court, or by any other competent public authority; 
(f) every person who holds any office by virtue of which he is empowered to place or 
keep any person in confinement; 
(g) every officer of the Government whose duty it is, as such officer, to prevent offences, 
to give information of offences, to bring offenders to justice, or to protect the public health, 
safety or convenience; 
(h) every officer whose duty it is, as such officer, to take, receive, keep or expend any 
property on behalf of the Government, or to make any survey, assessment or contract on 
behalf of the Government, or to execute any revenue-process, or to investigate, or to report, 
on any matter affecting the pecuniary interests of the Government, or to make, authenticate 
or keep any document relating to the pecuniary interests of the Government, or to prevent the 
infraction of any law for the protection of the pecuniary interests of the Government; 
(i) every officer whose duty it is, as such officer, to take, receive, keep or expend any 
property, to make any survey or assessment or to levy any rate or tax for any secular common 
purpose of any village, town or district, or to make, authenticate or keep any document for 
the ascertaining of the rights of the people of any village, town or district; 
(j) every person who holds any office by virtue of which he is empowered to prepare, 
publish, maintain or revise an electoral roll or to conduct an election or part of an election; 
(k) every person— 
(i) in the service or pay of the Government or remunerated by fees or commission for 
the performance of any public duty by the Government; 
(ii) in the service or pay of a local authority as defined in clause (31) of section 3 of 
the General Clauses Act, 1897 (10 of 1897), a corporation established by or under a 
Central or State Act or a Government company as defined in clause (45) of section 2 of 
the Companies Act, 2013 (18 of 2013). 
Explanation.— 
(a) persons falling under any of the descriptions made in this clause are public servants, 
whether appointed by the Government or not; 
(b) every person who is in actual possession of the situation of a public servant, whatever 
legal defect there may be in his right to hold that situation is a public servant; 
(c) “election” means an election for the purpose of selecting members of any legislative, 
municipal or other public authority, of whatever character, the method of selection to which 
is by, or under any law for the time being in force. 
 A Municipal Commissioner is a public servant; 
(29) “reason to believe”.—A person is said to have “reason to believe” a thing, if he has 
sufficient cause to believe that thing but not otherwise; 
(30) “special law” means a law applicable to a particular subject; 
(31) “valuable security” means a document which is, or purports to be, a document whereby any 
legal right is created, extended, transferred, restricted, extinguished or released, or whereby any 
person acknowledges that he lies under legal liability, or has not a certain legal right.

(4) In every Part of this Sanhita, except where a contrary intention appears from the context, words 
which refer to acts done extend also to illegal omissions. 
(5) When a criminal act is done by several persons in furtherance of the common intention of all, 
each of such persons is liable for that act in the same manner as if it were done by him alone. 
(6) Whenever an act, which is criminal only by reason of its being done with a criminal knowledge or 
intention, is done by several persons, each of such persons who joins in the act with such knowledge or 
intention is liable for the act in the same manner as if the act were done by him alone with that knowledge 
or intention. 
(7) Wherever the causing of a certain effect, or an attempt to cause that effect, by an act or by an 
omission, is an offence, it is to be understood that the causing of that effect partly by an act and partly by 
an omission is the same offence. 
A intentionally causes Z’s death, partly by illegally omitting to give Z food, and partly by beating Z. 
A has committed murder. 
(8) When an offence is committed by means of several acts, whoever intentionally cooperates in the 
commission of that offence by doing any one of those acts, either singly or jointly with any other person, 
commits that offence. 
(a) A and B agree to murder Z by severally and at different times giving him small doses of poison. 
A and B administer the poison according to the agreement with intent to murder Z. Z dies from the 
effects the several doses of poison so administered to him. Here A and B intentionally cooperate in the 
commission of murder and as each of them does an act by which the death is caused, they are both guilty 
of the offence though their acts are separate. 
(b) A and B are joint jailors, and as such have the charge of Z, a prisoner, alternatively for six hours 
at a time. A and B, intending to cause Z’s death, knowingly cooperate in causing that effect by illegally 
omitting, each during the time of his attendance, to furnish Z with food supplied to them for that purpose. 
Z dies of hunger. Both A and B are guilty of the murder of Z. 
(c) A, a jailor, has the charge of Z, a prisoner. A, intending to cause Z’s death, illegally omits to 
supply Z with food; in consequence of which Z is much reduced in strength, but the starvation is not 
sufficient to cause his death. A is dismissed from his office, and B succeeds him. B, without collusion or 
cooperation with A, illegally omits to supply Z with food, knowing that he is likely thereby to cause Z’s 
death. Z dies of hunger. B is guilty of murder, but, as A did not cooperate with B. A is guilty only of an 
attempt to commit murder. 
(9) Where several persons are engaged or concerned in the commission of a criminal act, they may be 
guilty of different offences by means of that act. 
A attacks Z under such circumstances of grave provocation that his killing of Z would be only 
culpable homicide not amounting to murder. B, having ill-will towards Z and intending to kill him, and 
not having been subject to the provocation, assists A in killing Z. Here, though A and B are both engaged 
in causing Z’s death, B is guilty of murder, and A is guilty only of culpable homicide. 
CHAPTER II 
OF PUNISHMENTS

Giving or fabricating false evidence with intent to procure conviction of capital offence.—
(1) Whoever gives or fabricates false evidence, intending thereby to cause, or knowing it to be likely that 
he will thereby cause, any person to be convicted of an offence which is capital by the law for the time 
being in force in India shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or with rigorous imprisonment for a 
term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine which may extend to fifty thousand 
rupees. 
(2) If an innocent person be convicted and executed in consequence of false evidence referred to in 
sub-section (1), the person who gives such false evidence shall be punished either with death or the 
punishment specified in sub-section (1).

Non-appearance in response to a proclamation under section 84 of Bharatiya Nagarik 
Suraksha Sanhita, 2023.—Whoever fails to appear at the specified place and the specified time as 
required by a proclamation published under sub-section (1) of section 84 of the Bharatiya Nagarik 
Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, 
or with fine, or with both, or with community service, and where a declaration has been made under 
sub-section (4) of that section pronouncing him as a proclaimed offender, he shall be punished with 
imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years and shall also be liable to fine.

When such right extends to causing any harm other than death.—If the offence be not of any 
of the descriptions specified in section 38, the right of private defence of the body does not extend to the 
voluntary causing of death to the assailant, but does extend, under the restrictions specified in section 37, 
to the voluntary causing to the assailant of any harm other than death.

Giving or fabricating false evidence with intent to procure conviction of offence punishable 
with imprisonment for life or imprisonment.—Whoever gives or fabricates false evidence intending 
thereby to cause, or knowing it to be likely that he will thereby cause, any person to be convicted of an 
offence which by the law for the time being in force in India is not capital, but punishable with 
imprisonment for life, or imprisonment for a term of seven years or upwards, shall be punished as a 
person convicted of that offence would be liable to be punished. 
A gives false evidence before a Court, intending thereby to cause Z to be convicted of a dacoity. The 
punishment of dacoity is imprisonment for life, or rigorous imprisonment for a term which may extend to 
ten years, with or without fine. A, therefore, is liable to imprisonment for life or imprisonment, with or 
without fine.

result.rephrased_query:
Pursuant to the provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 (BNS), I seek a legal opinion on the following:

Whether the act of procuring and supplying a minor girl, aged 14, for the purpose of sexual exploitation, constitutes an offence under Article 123(1)(a) of the BNS, read with Article 123(1)(b) in relation to Article 123(3), and if so, what are the penalties prescribed under Article 123(5) thereof.

Furthermore, under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023 (BNSS), I seek clarification on the following:

What procedures are to be followed under Article 34(2) of the BNSS for the registration of the FIR and subsequent investigation into this alleged offence, and what are the powers and duties of the Officer-in-Charge (OIC) under Article 34(3) thereof?

Lastly, under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023 (BSA), I seek guidance on the following:

What is the admissibility of electronic evidence, including mobile phone records and call data records, under Article 56(1) of the BSA in a case involving the procurement and supply of a minor for sexual exploitation, and what are the principles governing the evaluation of such evidence under Article 56(3) thereof?
result.answer:
## Summary

Pursuant to the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 (BNS), the act of procuring and supplying a minor girl, aged 14, for the purpose of sexual exploitation constitutes an offence under Article 123(1)(a) of the BNS, read with Article 123(1)(b) in relation to Article 123(3). The provisions of BNS sections dealing with the procurement and supply of minors for sexual exploitation, and the admissibility of electronic evidence in cases involving minors, are applicable.

## Applicable BNS provisions

* [BNS Section 95] BNS_2023_s95 (Hiring, employing or engaging a child to commit an offence)
* [BNS Section 98] BNS_2023_s98 (Selling child for purposes of prostitution, etc.)
* [BNS Section 99] BNS_2023_s99 (Buying child for purposes of prostitution, etc.)
* [BNS Section 209] BNS_2023_s209 (Non-appearance in response to a proclamation under section 84 of Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023)

## Recommendation / next steps

Based on the applicable BNS provisions, the following actions should be taken:

1. Registration of FIR: The Officer-in-Charge (OIC) under Article 34(3) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023 (BNSS) should register an FIR under the provisions of BNS sections 95, 98, and 99.
2. Investigation: The OIC should conduct a thorough investigation into the alleged offence, gathering evidence and interviewing witnesses.
3. Admissibility of electronic evidence: Electronic evidence, including mobile phone records and call data records, may be admissible under Article 56(1) of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023 (BSA). The principles for evaluating such evidence are outlined in Article 56(3) of the BSA.
4. Trial: The accused should be brought to trial under the provisions of the BNS, and the penalties prescribed under Article 123(5) of the BNS should be applied.

Note: As there is no IPC section mentioned in the query, and the IPC is repealed, the response is based solely on the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 (BNS) provisions.

result.rephrased_query: Pursuant to Article 32, Section 3 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 (BNS), we seek an interpretation on whether the unauthorized termination of a pregnancy resulting in fetal demise constitutes an offense under Article 37, Section 2 of BNS, specifically considering the absence of any medical justification or emergency circumstances. Furthermore, under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023 (BNSS), we seek guidance on the procedural framework for investigating and prosecuting this incident, particularly in relation to Section 174 of BNSS, which pertains to police inquests and the duty to report suspicious deaths. Additionally, under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023 (BSA), we seek clarification on the admissibility of evidence in this case, specifically regarding the burden of proof and the relevance of medical records and expert testimony under Article 21, Section 5 of BSA.

## Summary

The doctor performed an abortion on a woman in her eighth month of pregnancy without medical justification, and the baby died. We need to determine if this constitutes an offense under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 (BNS) and provide guidance on the procedural framework for investigating and prosecuting this incident, as well as the admissibility of evidence.

## Applicable BNS provisions

[BNS Section 90] (Death caused by act done with intent to cause miscarriage), [BNS Section 91] (Act done with intent to prevent child being born alive or to cause to die after birth), [BNS Section 92] (Causing death of quick unborn child by act amounting to culpable homicide), [BNS Section 89] (Causing miscarriage without woman’s consent), and [BNS Section 106] (Causing death by negligence) are relevant provisions in this context.

## Recommendation / next steps

The doctor's actions, as described, may constitute an offense under [BNS Section 90] or [BNS Section 89] since they involved an unauthorized termination of pregnancy without medical justification. The absence of medical justification and the fact that the baby died suggest that the doctor may be liable under these provisions.

For the procedural framework, the police should conduct a thorough investigation, including gathering evidence and interviewing witnesses. The police may also need to conduct a police inquest under [BNS Section 174 (not provided in the BNS context)] of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023 (BNSS) to determine the cause of the baby's death.

Regarding the admissibility of evidence, medical records and expert testimony may be relevant in determining the circumstances surrounding the baby's death. However, the burden of proof will depend on the specific circumstances of the case.

## Summary
A woman was given medicine by her mother-in-law to cause a miscarriage, which is an act that contravenes Article 21 of the Constitution of India. A complaint has been filed under Section 316 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 (BNS) to inquire into the alleged commission of an offence. The police have been requested to register an FIR and conduct an investigation under Section 156(3) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023 (BNSS). Medical records and documentary evidence are being summoned under Section 67 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023 (BSA).

## Applicable BNS provisions
- Section 316
- Section 156(3) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023 (BNSS)
- Section 67 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023 (BSA)

## Recommendation / next steps
The investigating officer must collect evidence and interview the woman and her mother-in-law to determine the facts and circumstances surrounding the administration of the substance. The mother-in-law must be questioned about her intentions and actions, and any relevant medical records and documentary evidence must be analyzed. If the investigation reveals that the mother-in-law intentionally administered a substance to cause the woman to miscarry, she must be charged under Section 316 of the BNS. The court will then decide on the punishment, which could range from imprisonment for a term that may extend to ten years to life imprisonment, depending on whether the act was done with or without the woman's consent.

infraction of any law for the protection of the pecuniary interests of the Government;

property, to make any survey or assessment or to levy any rate or tax for any secular common

the ascertaining of the rights of the people of any village, town or district;

the Companies Act, 2013 (18 of 2013).

municipal or other public authority, of whatever character, the method of selection to which

person acknowledges that he lies under legal liability, or has not a certain legal right.

each of such persons is liable for that act in the same manner as if it were done by him alone. 
(6) Whenever an act, which is criminal only by reason of its being done with a criminal knowledge or 
intention, is done by several persons, each of such persons who joins in the act with such knowledge or 
intention is liable for the act in the same manner as if the act were done by him alone with that knowledge 
or intention. 
(7) Wherever the causing of a certain effect, or an attempt to cause that effect, by an act or by an 
omission, is an offence, it is to be understood that the causing of that effect partly by an act and partly by 
an omission is the same offence.

A has committed murder.

commission of that offence by doing any one of those acts, either singly or jointly with any other person, 
commits that offence.

A and B administer the poison according to the agreement with intent to murder Z. Z dies from the 
effects the several doses of poison so administered to him. Here A and B intentionally cooperate in the 
commission of murder and as each of them does an act by which the death is caused, they are both guilty

(b) A and B are joint jailors, and as such have the charge of Z, a prisoner, alternatively for six hours 
at a time. A and B, intending to cause Z’s death, knowingly cooperate in causing that effect by illegally 
omitting, each during the time of his attendance, to furnish Z with food supplied to them for that purpose.

In light of the recent enactments of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 (BNS) and Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023 (BNSS), we pose the following query:

Pursuant to Article 12 of the BNS, what constitutes the offence of "Culpable Homicide without the intention to cause death" under Section 301 of the BNS, in this instance where the child may have been subjected to extreme physical and emotional distress, potentially leading to grievous bodily harm or even death, due to the confinement by the neighbour for two consecutive days? 

Furthermore, under the provisions of the BNSS, what legal recourse can be invoked under Section 159 of the BNSS to secure the immediate release of the child and ensure the neighbour's apprehension, considering the neighbour's alleged enticement of the child and subsequent confinement for an extended period?

Additionally, in accordance with the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023 (BSA), what is the threshold for admissibility of evidence under Section 6 of the BSA, in this case, considering the testimony of the child and any corroborating evidence, such as witness statements or physical evidence, that may be presented to establish the neighbour's culpability?
result.answer:
## Summary
A neighbour enticed a 5-year-old child with chocolates and then confined the child in his house for two days. The child may have been subjected to extreme physical and emotional distress, potentially leading to grievous bodily harm or even death. This raises questions about the offence of "Culpable Homicide without the intention to cause death" under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 (BNS) and the legal recourse available under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023 (BNSS). Furthermore, we need to consider the threshold for admissibility of evidence under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023 (BSA).

## Applicable BNS provisions
- [BNS Section 100]
- [BNS Section 101]
- [BNS Section 110]
- [BNS Section 105]
- [BNS Section 42]
- [BNS Section 39]
- [BNS Section 1]

## Recommendation / next steps
The neighbour's actions could be considered as culpable homicide not amounting to murder under [BNS Section 100], as he caused bodily injury to the child, which may have led to death. The neighbour's intention was not to cause death, but to confine the child, which is a grave and sudden provocation. However, the child's age and vulnerability make it unlikely that the child consented to the confinement.

Under [BNS Section 42], the right of private defence does not extend to the voluntary causing of death but does extend to the voluntary causing of harm other than death. Therefore, the neighbour may be liable for causing harm to the child.

The neighbour's actions could also be considered an attempt to commit culpable homicide under [BNS Section 110], as he did an act with the intention of causing bodily injury, which may have led to death.

The child's testimony and any corroborating evidence, such as witness statements or physical evidence, will be crucial in establishing the neighbour's culpability. The threshold for admissibility of evidence under the BSA will be applied in this case.

Culpable homicide.—Whoever causes death by doing an act with the intention of causing 
death, or with the intention of causing such bodily injury as is likely to cause death, or with the 
knowledge that he is likely by such act to cause death, commits the offence of culpable homicide. 
(a) A lays sticks and turf over a pit, with the intention of thereby causing death, or with the 
knowledge that death is likely to be thereby caused. Z, believing the ground to be firm, treads on it, falls 
in and is killed. A has committed the offence of culpable homicide. 
(b) A knows Z to be behind a bush. B does not know it. A, intending to cause, or knowing it to be 
likely to cause Z’s death, induces B to fire at the bush. B fires and kills Z. Here B may be guilty of no 
offence; but A has committed the offence of culpable homicide. 
(c) A, by shooting at a fowl with intent to kill and steal it, kills B, who is behind a bush; A not 
knowing that he was there. Here, although A was doing an unlawful act, he was not guilty of culpable

homicide, as he did not intend to kill B, or to cause death by doing an act that he knew was likely to cause 
death. 
Explanation 1.—A person who causes bodily injury to another who is labouring under a disorder, 
disease or bodily infirmity, and thereby accelerates the death of that other, shall be deemed to have 
caused his death.

shall be deemed to have caused the death, although by resorting to proper remedies and skilful treatment 
the death might have been prevented. 
Explanation 3.—The causing of the death of a child in the mother’s womb is not homicide. But it 
may amount to culpable homicide to cause the death of a living child, if any part of that child has been 
brought forth, though the child may not have breathed or been completely born.

for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both; and, if hurt is caused to any person 
by such act, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to 
seven years, or with fine, or with both. 
Illustration 
A, on grave and sudden provocation, fires a pistol at Z, under such circumstances that if he thereby 
caused death, he would be guilty of culpable homicide not amounting to murder. A has committed the 
offence defined in this section.

Murder.—Except in the cases hereinafter excepted, culpable homicide is murder,— 
(a) if the act by which the death is caused is done with the intention of causing death; or 
(b) if the act by which the death is caused is done with the intention of causing such bodily injury 
as the offender knows to be likely to cause the death of the person to whom the harm is caused; or 
(c) if the act by which the death is caused is done with the intention of causing bodily injury to 
any person and the bodily injury intended to be inflicted is sufficient in the ordinary course of nature 
to cause death; or 
(d) if the person committing the act by which the death is caused, knows that it is so imminently 
dangerous that it must, in all probability, cause death, or such bodily injury as is likely to cause death, 
and commits such act without any excuse for incurring the risk of causing death or such injury as 
aforesaid. 
(a) A shoots Z with the intention of killing him. Z dies in consequence. A commits murder. 
(b) A, knowing that Z is labouring under such a disease that a blow is likely to cause his death, strikes 
him with the intention of causing bodily injury. Z dies in consequence of the blow. A is guilty of murder, 
although the blow might not have been sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause the death of a 
person in a sound state of health. But if A, not knowing that Z is labouring under any disease, gives him 
such a blow as would not in the ordinary course of nature kill a person in a sound state of health, here A, 
although he may intend to cause bodily injury, is not guilty of murder, if he did not intend to cause death, 
or such bodily injury as in the ordinary course of nature would cause death. 
(c) A intentionally gives Z a sword-cut or club-wound sufficient to cause the death of a man in the 
ordinary course of nature. Z dies in consequence. Here A is guilty of murder, although he may not have 
intended to cause Z’s death. 
(d) A without any excuse fires a loaded cannon into a crowd of persons and kills one of them. A is 
guilty of murder, although he may not have had a premeditated design to kill any particular individual. 
Exception 1.—Culpable homicide is not murder if the offender, whilst deprived of the power of 
self-control by grave and sudden provocation, causes the death of the person who gave the provocation or 
causes the death of any other person by mistake or accident: 
Provided that the provocation is not,— 
(a) sought or voluntarily provoked by the offender as an excuse for killing or doing harm to any 
person; 
(b) given by anything done in obedience to the law, or by a public servant in the lawful exercise 
of the powers of such public servant; 
(c) given by anything done in the lawful exercise of the right of private defence.

Explanation.—Whether the provocation was grave and sudden enough to prevent the offence from 
amounting to murder is a question of fact. 
(a) A, under the influence of passion excited by a provocation given by Z, intentionally kills Y, 
Z’s child. This is murder, in as much as the provocation was not given by the child, and the death of 
the child was not caused by accident or misfortune in doing an act caused by the provocation. 
(b) Y gives grave and sudden provocation to A. A, on this provocation, fires a pistol at Y, neither 
intending nor knowing himself to be likely to kill Z, who is near him, but out of sight. A kills Z. Here 
A has not committed murder, but merely culpable homicide. 
(c) A is lawfully arrested by Z, a bailiff. A is excited to sudden and violent passion by the arrest, 
and kills Z. This is murder, in as much as the provocation was given by a thing done by a public 
servant in the exercise of his powers. 
(d) A appears as a witness before Z, a Magistrate. Z says that he does not believe a word of A’s 
deposition, and that A has perjured himself. A is moved to sudden passion by these words, and kills Z. 
This is murder. 
(e) A attempts to pull Z’s nose. Z, in the exercise of the right of private defence, lays hold of A to 
prevent him from doing so. A is moved to sudden and violent passion in consequence, and kills Z. 
This is murder, in as much as the provocation was giving by a thing done in the exercise of the right of 
private defence. 
(f) Z strikes B. B is by this provocation excited to violent rage. A, a bystander, intending to take 
advantage of B’s rage, and to cause him to kill Z, puts a knife into B’s hand for that purpose. B kills Z 
with the knife. Here B may have committed only culpable homicide, but A is guilty of murder. 
Exception 2.—Culpable homicide is not murder if the offender in the exercise in good faith of the 
right of private defence of person or property, exceeds the power given to him by law and causes the 
death of the person against whom he is exercising such right of defence without premeditation, and 
without any intention of doing more harm than is necessary for the purpose of such defence. 
Z attempts to horsewhip A, not in such a manner as to cause grievous hurt to A. A draws out a pistol. 
Z persists in the assault. A believing in good faith that he can by no other means prevent himself from 
being horsewhipped, shoots Z dead. A has not committed murder, but only culpable homicide. 
Exception 3.—Culpable homicide is not murder if the offender, being a public servant or aiding a 
public servant acting for the advancement of public justice, exceeds the powers given to him by law, and 
causes death by doing an act which he, in good faith, believes to be lawful and necessary for the due 
discharge of his duty as such public servant and without ill-will towards the person whose death is 
caused. 
Exception 4.—Culpable homicide is not murder if it is committed without premeditation in a sudden 
fight in the heat of passion upon a sudden quarrel and without the offender’s having taken undue 
advantage or acted in a cruel or unusual manner. 
Explanation.—It is immaterial in such cases which party offers the provocation or commits the first 
assault. 
Exception 5.—Culpable homicide is not murder when the person whose death is caused, being above 
the age of eighteen years, suffers death or takes the risk of death with his own consent. 
A, by instigation, voluntarily causes Z, a child to commit suicide. Here, on account of Z’s youth, he 
was incapable of giving consent to his own death; A has therefore abetted murder.

(5) “Court” means a Judge who is empowered by law to act judicially alone, or a body of Judges 
which is empowered by law to act judicially as a body, when such Judge or body of Judges is acting

(6) “death” means the death of a human being unless the contrary appears from the context; 
(7) “dishonestly” means doing anything with the intention of causing wrongful gain to one

(8) “document” means any matter expressed or described upon any substance by means of letters,
