(a) A writing expressing the terms of a contract, which may be used as evidence of the contract, 
is a document. 
(b) A cheque upon a banker is a document. 
(c) A power-of-attorney is a document. 
(d) A map or plan which is intended to be used or which may be used as evidence, is a document. 
(e) A writing containing directions or instructions is a document. 
Explanation 2.—Whatever is expressed by means of letters, figures or marks as explained by 
mercantile or other usage, shall be deemed to be expressed by such letters, figures or marks within 
the meaning of this section, although the same may not be actually expressed. 
A writes his name on the back of a bill of exchange payable to his order. The meaning of the 
endorsement, as explained by mercantile usage, is that the bill is to be paid to the holder. The 
endorsement is a document, and shall be construed in the same manner as if the words “pay to the 
holder” or words to that effect had been written over the signature; 
(9) “fraudulently” means doing anything with the intention to defraud but not otherwise; 
(10) “gender”.—The pronoun “he” and its derivatives are used of any person, whether male, 
female or transgender. 
Explanation.–– “transgender” shall have the meaning assigned to it in clause (k) of section 2 of 
the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 (40 of 2019); 
(11) “good faith”.—Nothing is said to be done or believed in “good faith” which is done or 
believed without due care and attention; 
(12) “Government” means the Central Government or a State Government; 
(13) “harbour” includes supplying a person with shelter, food, drink, money, clothes, arms,

(14) “injury” means any harm whatever illegally caused to any person, in body, mind, reputation 
or property; 
(15) “illegal” and “legally bound to do”.—The word “illegal” is applicable to everything which is 
an offence or which is prohibited by law, or which furnishes ground for a civil action; and a person is 
said to be “legally bound to do” whatever it is illegal in him to omit;

execute any judicial process, or to administer any oath, or to interpret, or to preserve order in

(d) every assessor or member of a panchayat assisting a Court or public servant; 
(e) every arbitrator or other person to whom any cause or matter has been referred for

(f) every person who holds any office by virtue of which he is empowered to place or 
keep any person in confinement; 
(g) every officer of the Government whose duty it is, as such officer, to prevent offences, 
to give information of offences, to bring offenders to justice, or to protect the public health, 
safety or convenience; 
(h) every officer whose duty it is, as such officer, to take, receive, keep or expend any 
property on behalf of the Government, or to make any survey, assessment or contract on 
behalf of the Government, or to execute any revenue-process, or to investigate, or to report, 
on any matter affecting the pecuniary interests of the Government, or to make, authenticate 
or keep any document relating to the pecuniary interests of the Government, or to prevent the 
infraction of any law for the protection of the pecuniary interests of the Government; 
(i) every officer whose duty it is, as such officer, to take, receive, keep or expend any 
property, to make any survey or assessment or to levy any rate or tax for any secular common

the ascertaining of the rights of the people of any village, town or district; 
(j) every person who holds any office by virtue of which he is empowered to prepare, 
publish, maintain or revise an electoral roll or to conduct an election or part of an election;

(i) in the service or pay of the Government or remunerated by fees or commission for 
the performance of any public duty by the Government; 
(ii) in the service or pay of a local authority as defined in clause (31) of section 3 of 
the General Clauses Act, 1897 (10 of 1897), a corporation established by or under a 
Central or State Act or a Government company as defined in clause (45) of section 2 of 
the Companies Act, 2013 (18 of 2013). 
Explanation.— 
(a) persons falling under any of the descriptions made in this clause are public servants, 
whether appointed by the Government or not; 
(b) every person who is in actual possession of the situation of a public servant, whatever 
legal defect there may be in his right to hold that situation is a public servant; 
(c) “election” means an election for the purpose of selecting members of any legislative, 
municipal or other public authority, of whatever character, the method of selection to which 
is by, or under any law for the time being in force. 
 A Municipal Commissioner is a public servant; 
(29) “reason to believe”.—A person is said to have “reason to believe” a thing, if he has 
sufficient cause to believe that thing but not otherwise; 
(30) “special law” means a law applicable to a particular subject; 
(31) “valuable security” means a document which is, or purports to be, a document whereby any 
legal right is created, extended, transferred, restricted, extinguished or released, or whereby any 
person acknowledges that he lies under legal liability, or has not a certain legal right.

(4) In every Part of this Sanhita, except where a contrary intention appears from the context, words 
which refer to acts done extend also to illegal omissions. 
(5) When a criminal act is done by several persons in furtherance of the common intention of all, 
each of such persons is liable for that act in the same manner as if it were done by him alone. 
(6) Whenever an act, which is criminal only by reason of its being done with a criminal knowledge or 
intention, is done by several persons, each of such persons who joins in the act with such knowledge or 
intention is liable for the act in the same manner as if the act were done by him alone with that knowledge 
or intention. 
(7) Wherever the causing of a certain effect, or an attempt to cause that effect, by an act or by an 
omission, is an offence, it is to be understood that the causing of that effect partly by an act and partly by 
an omission is the same offence. 
A intentionally causes Z’s death, partly by illegally omitting to give Z food, and partly by beating Z. 
A has committed murder. 
(8) When an offence is committed by means of several acts, whoever intentionally cooperates in the 
commission of that offence by doing any one of those acts, either singly or jointly with any other person, 
commits that offence. 
(a) A and B agree to murder Z by severally and at different times giving him small doses of poison. 
A and B administer the poison according to the agreement with intent to murder Z. Z dies from the 
effects the several doses of poison so administered to him. Here A and B intentionally cooperate in the 
commission of murder and as each of them does an act by which the death is caused, they are both guilty 
of the offence though their acts are separate. 
(b) A and B are joint jailors, and as such have the charge of Z, a prisoner, alternatively for six hours 
at a time. A and B, intending to cause Z’s death, knowingly cooperate in causing that effect by illegally 
omitting, each during the time of his attendance, to furnish Z with food supplied to them for that purpose. 
Z dies of hunger. Both A and B are guilty of the murder of Z. 
(c) A, a jailor, has the charge of Z, a prisoner. A, intending to cause Z’s death, illegally omits to 
supply Z with food; in consequence of which Z is much reduced in strength, but the starvation is not 
sufficient to cause his death. A is dismissed from his office, and B succeeds him. B, without collusion or 
cooperation with A, illegally omits to supply Z with food, knowing that he is likely thereby to cause Z’s 
death. Z dies of hunger. B is guilty of murder, but, as A did not cooperate with B. A is guilty only of an 
attempt to commit murder. 
(9) Where several persons are engaged or concerned in the commission of a criminal act, they may be 
guilty of different offences by means of that act. 
A attacks Z under such circumstances of grave provocation that his killing of Z would be only 
culpable homicide not amounting to murder. B, having ill-will towards Z and intending to kill him, and 
not having been subject to the provocation, assists A in killing Z. Here, though A and B are both engaged 
in causing Z’s death, B is guilty of murder, and A is guilty only of culpable homicide. 
CHAPTER II 
OF PUNISHMENTS

Punishment for culpable homicide not amounting to murder.—Whoever commits culpable 
homicide not amounting to murder, shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or imprisonment of 
either description for a term which shall not be less than five years but which may extend to ten years, 
and shall also be liable to fine, if the act by which the death is caused is done with the intention of 
causing death, or of causing such bodily injury as is likely to cause death; or with imprisonment of either 
description for a term which may extend to ten years and with fine, if the act is done with the knowledge 
that it is likely to cause death, but without any intention to cause death, or to cause such bodily injury as 
is likely to cause death.

When such right extends to causing any harm other than death.—If the offence be not of any 
of the descriptions specified in section 38, the right of private defence of the body does not extend to the 
voluntary causing of death to the assailant, but does extend, under the restrictions specified in section 37, 
to the voluntary causing to the assailant of any harm other than death.

When such right extends to causing any harm other than death.—If the offence, the 
committing of which, or the attempting to commit which occasions the exercise of the right of private 
defence, be theft, mischief, or criminal trespass, not of any of the descriptions specified in section 41, that 
right does not extend to the voluntary causing of death, but does extend, subject to the restrictions 
specified in section 37, to the voluntary causing to the wrong-doer of any harm other than death.

Culpable homicide.—Whoever causes death by doing an act with the intention of causing 
death, or with the intention of causing such bodily injury as is likely to cause death, or with the 
knowledge that he is likely by such act to cause death, commits the offence of culpable homicide. 
(a) A lays sticks and turf over a pit, with the intention of thereby causing death, or with the 
knowledge that death is likely to be thereby caused. Z, believing the ground to be firm, treads on it, falls 
in and is killed. A has committed the offence of culpable homicide. 
(b) A knows Z to be behind a bush. B does not know it. A, intending to cause, or knowing it to be 
likely to cause Z’s death, induces B to fire at the bush. B fires and kills Z. Here B may be guilty of no 
offence; but A has committed the offence of culpable homicide. 
(c) A, by shooting at a fowl with intent to kill and steal it, kills B, who is behind a bush; A not 
knowing that he was there. Here, although A was doing an unlawful act, he was not guilty of culpable

homicide, as he did not intend to kill B, or to cause death by doing an act that he knew was likely to cause 
death. 
Explanation 1.—A person who causes bodily injury to another who is labouring under a disorder, 
disease or bodily infirmity, and thereby accelerates the death of that other, shall be deemed to have 
caused his death. 
Explanation 2.—Where death is caused by bodily injury, the person who causes such bodily injury 
shall be deemed to have caused the death, although by resorting to proper remedies and skilful treatment 
the death might have been prevented. 
Explanation 3.—The causing of the death of a child in the mother’s womb is not homicide. But it 
may amount to culpable homicide to cause the death of a living child, if any part of that child has been 
brought forth, though the child may not have breathed or been completely born.

Pursuant to Article 45 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 (BNS), a query is raised regarding the penal consequences for the dissemination of seditious material via online platforms, as described in Section 5, Sub-Section 2 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 (BNS), under the circumstances where several individuals have posted online manifestos calling upon others to take up arms against the Indian government, thereby potentially inciting violence and public disorder. 

Furthermore, under the provisions of Article 78 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023 (BNSS), it is sought to determine the procedure for investigating and prosecuting such offenses, including the powers of law enforcement agencies to seize digital evidence, Section 21, Sub-Section 1 of BNSS, and the requirements for obtaining search warrants in relation to online activities, Article 32 of BNSS.

Additionally, under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023 (BSA), the query seeks clarification on the admissibility of digital evidence, including online posts and manifests, as a form of proof in a court of law, particularly in relation to the principles outlined in Article 19 of BSA, regarding the weight to be assigned to circumstantial evidence.

## Summary

The user has described a scenario where a group posted online manifestos calling upon people to take up arms against the Indian government, potentially inciting violence and public disorder. This raises concerns under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 (BNS) regarding the penal consequences for the dissemination of seditious material via online platforms. The user has also inquired about the procedure for investigating and prosecuting such offenses, including the powers of law enforcement agencies to seize digital evidence, and the admissibility of digital evidence in a court of law.

## Applicable BNS provisions

[BNS Section 197]
[BNS Section 353]
[BNS Section 113]
[BNS Section 229]
[BNS Section 148]

## Recommendation / next steps

The dissemination of seditious material via online platforms, as described in the scenario, is likely to fall under the provisions of Section 197 of the BNS, which deals with imputations and assertions prejudicial to national integration. This section makes it an offense to make or publish any imputation or assertion that any class of persons cannot, by reason of their being members of any religious, racial, language or regional group or caste or community, bear true faith and allegiance to the Constitution of India as by law established or uphold the sovereignty and integrity of India.

Furthermore, Section 353 of the BNS deals with statements conducing to public mischief, which includes making, publishing or circulating any statement, false information, rumour or report that is likely to cause fear or alarm to the public, or to induce any person to commit an offense against the State or against the public tranquillity.

In terms of the procedure for investigating and prosecuting such offenses, the powers of law enforcement agencies to seize digital evidence are likely to be governed by the provisions of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023 (BNSS), specifically Section 21, Sub-Section 1. The admissibility of digital evidence in a court of law is also likely to be governed by the principles outlined in the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023 (BSA), specifically Article 19.

In terms of the penalty for such offenses, Section 113 of the BNS deals with terrorist acts, and Section 229 deals with punishment for false evidence. Section 148 deals with conspiracy to commit offenses punishable by Section 147.

Therefore, the next steps would be to investigate the online manifestos and gather evidence, and to prosecute the individuals involved under the relevant provisions of the BNS.

Short title, commencement and application.––(1) This Act may be called the Bharatiya Nyaya 
Sanhita, 2023. 
(2) It shall come into force on such date1 as the Central Government may, by notification in the 
Official Gazette, appoint, and different dates may be appointed for different provisions of this Sanhita. 
(3) Every person shall be liable to punishment under this Sanhita and not otherwise for every act or 
omission contrary to the provisions thereof, of which he shall be guilty within India. 
(4) Any person liable, by any law for the time being in force in India, to be tried for an offence 
committed beyond India shall be dealt with according to the provisions of this Sanhita for any act 
committed beyond India in the same manner as if such act had been committed within India. 
(5) The provisions of this Sanhita shall also apply to any offence committed by— 
(a) any citizen of India in any place without and beyond India; 
(b) any person on any ship or aircraft registered in India wherever it may be; 
(c) any person in any place without and beyond India committing offence targeting a computer 
resource located in India. 
Explanation.—In this section, the word “offence” includes every act committed outside India which, 
if committed in India, would be punishable under this Sanhita. 
A, who is a citizen of India, commits a murder in any place without and beyond India. 
He can be tried and convicted of murder in any place in India in which he may be found. 
(6) Nothing in this Sanhita shall affect the provisions of any Act for punishing mutiny and desertion 
of officers, soldiers, sailors or airmen in the service of the Government of India or the provisions of any 
special or local law.

Statements conducing to public mischief.—(1) Whoever makes, publishes or circulates any 
statement, false information, rumour, or report, including through electronic means— 
(a) with intent to cause, or which is likely to cause, any officer, soldier, sailor or airman in the 
Army, Navy or Air Force of India to mutiny or otherwise disregard or fail in his duty as such; or 
(b) with intent to cause, or which is likely to cause, fear or alarm to the public, or to any section 
of the public whereby any person may be induced to commit an offence against the State or against 
the public tranquillity; or 
(c) with intent to incite, or which is likely to incite, any class or community of persons to commit 
any offence against any other class or community, 
shall be punished with imprisonment which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. 
(2) Whoever makes, publishes or circulates any statement or report containing false information, 
rumour or alarming news, including through electronic means, with intent to create or promote, or which 
is likely to create or promote, on grounds of religion, race, place of birth, residence, language, caste or 
community or any other ground whatsoever, feelings of enmity, hatred or ill will between different 
religious, racial, language or regional groups or castes or communities, shall be punished with 
imprisonment which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. 
(3) Whoever commits an offence specified in sub-section (2) in any place of worship or in any 
assembly engaged in the performance of religious worship or religious ceremonies, shall be punished 
with imprisonment which may extend to five years and shall also be liable to fine. 
Exception.—It does not amount to an offence, within the meaning of this section, when the person 
making, publishing or circulating any such statement, false information, rumour or report, has reasonable 
grounds for believing that such statement, false information, rumour or report is true and makes, 
publishes or circulates it in good faith and without any such intent as aforesaid.

Now, it is proposed to enact a new law, namely, the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita Bill, 2023 by 
repealing the Indian Penal Code to streamline provisions relating to offences and penalties. It is proposed 
to provide first time community service as one of the punishments for petty offences. The offences 
against women and children, murder and offences against the State have been given precedence. The 
various offences have been made gender neutral. In order to deal effectively with the problem of 
organised crimes and terrorist activities, new offences of terrorist acts and organised crime have been 
added in the Bill with deterrent punishments. A new offence on acts of secession, armed rebellion, 
subversive activities, separatist activities or endangering sovereignty or unity and integrity of India has 
also been added. The fines and punishment for various offences have also been suitably enhanced.

Imputations, assertions prejudicial to national integration.—(1) Whoever, by words either 
spoken or written or by signs or by visible representations or through electronic communication or 
otherwise,— 
(a) makes or publishes any imputation that any class of persons cannot, by reason of their being 
members of any religious, racial, language or regional group or caste or community, bear true faith 
and allegiance to the Constitution of India as by law established or uphold the sovereignty and 
integrity of India; or

(b) asserts, counsels, advises, propagates or publishes that any class of persons shall, by reason of 
their being members of any religious, racial, language or regional group or caste or community, be 
denied, or deprived of their rights as citizens of India; or 
(c) makes or publishes any assertion, counsel, plea or appeal concerning the obligation of any 
class of persons, by reason of their being members of any religious, racial, language or regional 
group or caste or community, and such assertion, counsel, plea or appeal causes or is likely to cause 
disharmony or feelings of enmity or hatred or ill-will between such members and other persons; or 
(d) makes or publishes false or misleading information, jeopardising the sovereignty, unity and 
integrity or security of India, 
shall be punished with imprisonment which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. 
(2) Whoever commits an offence specified in sub-section (1) in any place of worship or in any 
assembly engaged in the performance of religious worship or religious ceremonies, shall be punished 
with imprisonment which may extend to five years and shall also be liable to fine.

intention, is done by several persons, each of such persons who joins in the act with such knowledge or 
intention is liable for the act in the same manner as if the act were done by him alone with that knowledge 
or intention.

omission, is an offence, it is to be understood that the causing of that effect partly by an act and partly by 
an omission is the same offence.

A has committed murder. 
(8) When an offence is committed by means of several acts, whoever intentionally cooperates in the 
commission of that offence by doing any one of those acts, either singly or jointly with any other person, 
commits that offence.

A and B administer the poison according to the agreement with intent to murder Z. Z dies from the 
effects the several doses of poison so administered to him. Here A and B intentionally cooperate in the 
commission of murder and as each of them does an act by which the death is caused, they are both guilty 
of the offence though their acts are separate. 
(b) A and B are joint jailors, and as such have the charge of Z, a prisoner, alternatively for six hours 
at a time. A and B, intending to cause Z’s death, knowingly cooperate in causing that effect by illegally 
omitting, each during the time of his attendance, to furnish Z with food supplied to them for that purpose. 
Z dies of hunger. Both A and B are guilty of the murder of Z. 
(c) A, a jailor, has the charge of Z, a prisoner. A, intending to cause Z’s death, illegally omits to 
supply Z with food; in consequence of which Z is much reduced in strength, but the starvation is not 
sufficient to cause his death. A is dismissed from his office, and B succeeds him. B, without collusion or 
cooperation with A, illegally omits to supply Z with food, knowing that he is likely thereby to cause Z’s 
death. Z dies of hunger. B is guilty of murder, but, as A did not cooperate with B. A is guilty only of an 
attempt to commit murder. 
(9) Where several persons are engaged or concerned in the commission of a criminal act, they may be 
guilty of different offences by means of that act.

culpable homicide not amounting to murder. B, having ill-will towards Z and intending to kill him, and 
not having been subject to the provocation, assists A in killing Z. Here, though A and B are both engaged 
in causing Z’s death, B is guilty of murder, and A is guilty only of culpable homicide.

Pursuant to BNS 2023, Article 193, Section 2, is the act of a candidate distributing cash and liquor to voters to secure their votes in a village election an instance of undue influence, corruption, or bribery as defined under the Act?

Further, under BNSS 2023, Article 34, Section 3, what are the applicable procedures for registration of a First Information Report (FIR) and subsequent investigation in this matter?

Additionally, under BSA 2023, Section 63, Article 12, what are the admissibility criteria for evidence of electronic transactions and eyewitness testimony in a court of law in this scenario?

A candidate distributed cash and liquor to voters to secure their votes in a village election. The question is whether this act constitutes undue influence, corruption, or bribery under BNS 2023.

- [BNS Section 174]
- [BNS Section 176]

- [BNS Section 337]
- [BNS Section 353]
- [BNS Section 1]

## Recommendation / next steps

Given the context, the act of a candidate distributing cash and liquor to voters to secure their votes in a village election can be considered as an instance of corrupt practice under [BNS Section 176]. 

To register a First Information Report (FIR), the procedures will involve reporting to the designated authorities, such as the village head or the police station. The FIR must be registered and investigated as per the BNS procedures.

Regarding the admissibility of evidence, electronic transactions and eyewitness testimony can be considered as admissible evidence in a court of law, as per [BNS Section 337]. However, the admissibility of such evidence will depend on the specific circumstances of the case and the court's discretion. 

It is recommended that the candidate's actions be investigated, and appropriate action be taken under the BNS 2023.

Pursuant to the provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 (BNS), a complaint is hereby submitted to investigate and prosecute the perpetrators of an alleged offence under Section 147 of the BNS, read with Section 153A of the BNS, for engaging in an unlawful assembly to cause harm to a particular community and promoting enmity between different groups on grounds of religion, respectively.

Furthermore, under the provisions of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023 (BNSS), the complainant seeks to invoke the powers of the Magistrate to issue necessary directions and orders to maintain public order, prevent further violence, and ensure the safety and security of the affected community, particularly under Article 128 of the BNSS and Article 135 of the BNSS.

In addition, the complainant requires assistance from the authorities to gather evidence and secure the same under the provisions of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023 (BSA), specifically to prove the identity of the perpetrators, their involvement in the commission of the offence, and the role of social media in spreading the rumour that led to the attack, as enshrined in Section 35 of the BSA and Article 21 of the BSA.

## Summary
A mob of 200 people armed with sticks and swords attacked shops belonging to a particular community after a rumour spread on social media. The complainant seeks to investigate and prosecute the perpetrators under Section 147 of the BNS for unlawful assembly and Section 153A of the BNS for promoting enmity between different groups on grounds of religion.

## Applicable BNS provisions
- [BNS Section 147]
- [BNS Section 153A]
- [BNS Section 353]
- [BNS Section 197]
- [BNS Section 299]

## Recommendation / next steps
Given the severity of the offense and the need for immediate action, the Magistrate should issue necessary directions and orders to maintain public order, prevent further violence, and ensure the safety and security of the affected community, as per Article 128 of the BNSS. The authorities should also assist in gathering evidence and securing the same to prove the identity of the perpetrators and their involvement in the commission of the offense, as enshrined in Section 35 of the BSA and Article 21 of the BSA.

Now, it is proposed to enact a new law, namely, the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita Bill, 2023 by 
repealing the Indian Penal Code to streamline provisions relating to offences and penalties. It is proposed 
to provide first time community service as one of the punishments for petty offences. The offences 
against women and children, murder and offences against the State have been given precedence. The 
various offences have been made gender neutral. In order to deal effectively with the problem of 
organised crimes and terrorist activities, new offences of terrorist acts and organised crime have been 
added in the Bill with deterrent punishments. A new offence on acts of secession, armed rebellion, 
subversive activities, separatist activities or endangering sovereignty or unity and integrity of India has 
also been added. The fines and punishment for various offences have also been suitably enhanced.

omission contrary to the provisions thereof, of which he shall be guilty within India. 
(4) Any person liable, by any law for the time being in force in India, to be tried for an offence 
committed beyond India shall be dealt with according to the provisions of this Sanhita for any act 
committed beyond India in the same manner as if such act had been committed within India.

(a) any citizen of India in any place without and beyond India; 
(b) any person on any ship or aircraft registered in India wherever it may be; 
(c) any person in any place without and beyond India committing offence targeting a computer 
resource located in India.

shall be punished with imprisonment which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both.

A and B administer the poison according to the agreement with intent to murder Z. Z dies from the 
effects the several doses of poison so administered to him. Here A and B intentionally cooperate in the 
commission of murder and as each of them does an act by which the death is caused, they are both guilty 
of the offence though their acts are separate.

at a time. A and B, intending to cause Z’s death, knowingly cooperate in causing that effect by illegally

cooperation with A, illegally omits to supply Z with food, knowing that he is likely thereby to cause Z’s 
death. Z dies of hunger. B is guilty of murder, but, as A did not cooperate with B. A is guilty only of an 
attempt to commit murder.

guilty of different offences by means of that act.

culpable homicide not amounting to murder. B, having ill-will towards Z and intending to kill him, and 
not having been subject to the provocation, assists A in killing Z. Here, though A and B are both engaged

## Summary
A man voted in the election using someone else's identity card and later the real voter was turned away at the booth.

## Applicable BNS provisions
- [BNS Section 172]
- [BNS Section 173]
- [BNS Section 337]
- [BNS Section 356]

## Recommendation / next steps
To investigate this alleged offense, the following steps should be taken:

1. Gather evidence under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023 (BSA) to determine its admissibility and probative value in establishing the facts of the case, particularly with regards to BSA Article 35(3), which deals with the authentication of documents.
2. Investigate whether the man's actions constitute an offense under BNS Article 173(1) and if the genuine voter's exclusion from the polling booth amounted to a violation of BNS Article 173(2).
3. Apply the provisions of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023 (BNSS) to investigate and prosecute this alleged offense.
4. Determine the admissibility of the evidence under BNS Section 337, considering the forgery of documents and the authenticity of the voter's identity card.
5. Consider the provisions of BNS Section 356, regarding defamation, if applicable, and BNS Section 175, regarding false statements in connection with an election.
6. If the man's actions are found to be in contravention of the law, proceed with the prosecution under BNS Section 174, which provides for punishment for undue influence or personation at an election.

False statement in connection with an election.—Whoever with intent to affect the result of 
an election makes or publishes any statement purporting to be a statement of fact which is false and 
which he either knows or believes to be false or does not believe to be true, in relation to the personal 
character or conduct of any candidate shall be punished with fine.

Defamation.—(1) Whoever, by words either spoken or intended to be read, or by signs or by 
visible representations, makes or publishes in any manner, any imputation concerning any person 
intending to harm, or knowing or having reason to believe that such imputation will harm, the reputation 
of such person, is said, except in the cases hereinafter excepted, to defame that person. 
Explanation 1.—It may amount to defamation to impute anything to a deceased person, if the 
imputation would harm the reputation of that person if living, and is intended to be hurtful to the feelings 
of his family or other near relatives. 
Explanation 2.—It may amount to defamation to make an imputation concerning a company or an 
association or collection of persons as such. 
Explanation 3.—An imputation in the form of an alternative or expressed ironically, may amount to 
defamation. 
Explanation 4.—No imputation is said to harm a person’s reputation, unless that imputation directly 
or indirectly, in the estimation of others, lowers the moral or intellectual character of that person, or 
lowers the character of that person in respect of his caste or of his calling, or lowers the credit of that 
person, or causes it to be believed that the body of that person is in a loathsome state, or in a state 
generally considered as disgraceful. 
(a) A says—“Z is an honest man; he never stole B’s watch”; intending to cause it to be believed that 
Z did steal B’s watch. This is defamation, unless it falls within one of the exceptions. 
(b) A is asked who stole B’s watch. A points to Z, intending to cause it to be believed that Z stole B’s 
watch. This is defamation, unless it falls within one of the exceptions. 
(c) A draws a picture of Z running away with B’s watch, intending it to be believed that Z stole B’s 
watch. This is defamation, unless it falls within one of the exceptions. 
Exception 1.—It is not defamation to impute anything which is true concerning any person, if it be 
for the public good that the imputation should be made or published. Whether or not it is for the public 
good is a question of fact. 
Exception 2.—It is not defamation to express in good faith any opinion whatever respecting the 
conduct of a public servant in the discharge of his public functions, or respecting his character, so far as 
his character appears in that conduct, and no further. 
Exception 3.—It is not defamation to express in good faith any opinion whatever respecting the 
conduct of any person touching any public question, and respecting his character, so far as his character 
appears in that conduct, and no further. 
It is not defamation in A to express in good faith any opinion whatever respecting Z’s conduct in 
petitioning Government on a public question, in signing a requisition for a meeting on a public question, 
in presiding or attending at such meeting, in forming or joining any society which invites the public 
support, in voting or canvassing for a particular candidate for any situation in the efficient discharge of 
the duties of which the public is interested.

Exception 4.—It is not defamation to publish substantially true report of the proceedings of a Court, 
or of the result of any such proceedings. 
Explanation.—A Magistrate or other officer holding an inquiry in open Court preliminary to a trial in 
a Court, is a Court within the meaning of the above section. 
Exception 5.—It is not defamation to express in good faith any opinion whatever respecting the 
merits of any case, civil or criminal, which has been decided by a Court, or respecting the conduct of any 
person as a party, witness or agent, in any such case, or respecting the character of such person, as far as 
his character appears in that conduct, and no further. 
(a) A says—“I think Z’s evidence on that trial is so contradictory that he must be stupid or 
dishonest”. A is within this exception if he says this in good faith, in as much as the opinion which he 
expresses respects Z’s character as it appears in Z’s conduct as a witness, and no further. 
(b) But if A says—“I do not believe what Z asserted at that trial because I know him to be a man 
without veracity”; A is not within this exception, in as much as the opinion which expresses of Z’s 
character, is an opinion not founded on Z’s conduct as a witness. 
Exception 6.—It is not defamation to express in good faith any opinion respecting the merits of any 
performance which its author has submitted to the judgment of the public, or respecting the character of 
the author so far as his character appears in such performance, and no further. 
Explanation.—A performance may be submitted to the judgment of the public expressly or by acts on 
the part of the author which imply such submission to the judgment of the public. 
(a) A person who publishes a book, submits that book to the judgment of the public. 
(b) A person who makes a speech in public, submits that speech to the judgment of the public. 
(c) An actor or singer who appears on a public stage, submits his acting or singing to the judgment of 
the public. 
(d) A says of a book published by Z—“Z’s book is foolish; Z must be a weak man. Z’s book is 
indecent; Z must be a man of impure mind”. A is within the exception, if he says this in good faith, in as 
much as the opinion which he expresses of Z respects Z’s character only so far as it appears in Z’s book, 
and no further. 
(e) But if A says “I am not surprised that Z’s book is foolish and indecent, for he is a weak man and a 
libertine”. A is not within this exception, in as much as the opinion which he expresses of Z’s character is 
an opinion not founded on Z’s book. 
Exception 7.—It is not defamation in a person having over another any authority, either conferred by 
law or arising out of a lawful contract made with that other, to pass in good faith any censure on the 
conduct of that other in matters to which such lawful authority relates. 
A Judge censuring in good faith the conduct of a witness, or of an officer of the Court; a head of a 
department censuring in good faith those who are under his orders, a parent censuring in good faith a 
child in the presence of other children; a school master, whose authority is derived from a parent, 
censuring in good faith a pupil in the presence of other pupils; a master censuring a servant in good faith 
for remissness in service; a banker censuring in good faith the cashier of his bank for the conduct of such 
cashier as such cashier are within this exception. 
Exception 8.—It is not defamation to prefer in good faith an accusation against any person to any of 
those who have lawful authority over that person with respect to the subject-matter of accusation.

If A in good faith accuses Z before a Magistrate; if A in good faith complains of the conduct of Z, a 
servant, to Z’s master; if A in good faith complains of the conduct of Z, a child, to Z’s father, A is within 
this exception. 
Exception 9.—It is not defamation to make an imputation on the character of another provided that 
the imputation be made in good faith for the protection of the interests of the person making it, or of any 
other person, or for the public good. 
(a) A, a shopkeeper, says to B, who manages his business—“Sell nothing to Z unless he pays you 
ready money, for I have no opinion of his honesty”. A is within the exception, if he has made this 
imputation on Z in good faith for the protection of his own interests. 
(b) A, a Magistrate, in making a report to his own superior officer, casts an imputation on the 
character of Z. Here, if the imputation is made in good faith, and for the public good, A is within the 
exception. 
Exception 10.—It is not defamation to convey a caution, in good faith, to one person against another, 
provided that such caution be intended for the good of the person to whom it is conveyed, or of some 
person in whom that person is interested, or for the public good. 
(2) Whoever defames another shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may 
extend to two years, or with fine, or with both, or with community service. 
(3) Whoever prints or engraves any matter, knowing or having good reason to believe that such

servant in his official capacity, or an authority to institute or defend a suit, or to take any proceedings

therein, or to confess judgment, or a power of attorney, shall be punished with imprisonment of either 
Explanation.—For the purposes of this section, “register” includes any list, data or record of any

Imputations, assertions prejudicial to national integration.—(1) Whoever, by words either 
spoken or written or by signs or by visible representations or through electronic communication or

(a) makes or publishes any imputation that any class of persons cannot, by reason of their being

their being members of any religious, racial, language or regional group or caste or community, be

(c) makes or publishes any assertion, counsel, plea or appeal concerning the obligation of any

(d) makes or publishes false or misleading information, jeopardising the sovereignty, unity and 
integrity or security of India, 
shall be punished with imprisonment which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. 
(2) Whoever commits an offence specified in sub-section (1) in any place of worship or in any 
assembly engaged in the performance of religious worship or religious ceremonies, shall be punished 
with imprisonment which may extend to five years and shall also be liable to fine. 

CHAPTER XII 
OF OFFENCES BY OR RELATING TO PUBLIC SERVANTS

Personation at elections.—Whoever at an election applies for a voting paper on votes in the 
name of any other person, whether living or dead, or in a fictitious name, or who having voted once at 
such election applies at the same election for a voting paper in his own name, and whoever abets, 
procures or attempts to procure the voting by any person in any such way, commits the offence of 
personation at an election: 
Provided that nothing in this section shall apply to a person who has been authorised to vote as proxy 
for an elector under any law for the time being in force in so far as he votes as a proxy for such elector.

Punishment for undue influence or personation at an election.—Whoever commits the 
offence of undue influence or personation at an election shall be punished with imprisonment of either 
description for a term which may extend to one year or with fine, or with both.

result.rephrased_query: Pursuant to the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 (BNS), can a public incitement case be registered against the political leader under Article 304 (1) of the BNS for promoting enmity between different groups on grounds of religion and doing acts prejudicial to the maintenance of harmony, read with Article 123 of the BNS for the provision of public incitement to violence, and can the leader be held liable under Article 306 of the BNS for criminal conspiracy, in light of the provisions of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023 (BSA) regarding the admissibility of speech recordings and statements made in public as evidence, and the applicable provisions of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023 (BNSS) regarding the procedure for registration of a First Information Report (FIR) and subsequent investigation, as well as the applicable provisions for the arrest and custody of the accused leader?
result.answer:
## Summary

A political leader gave a speech inciting Hindus and Muslims to fight each other and burn each other's shops. The question arises whether a public incitement case can be registered against the leader under the relevant provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS).

## Applicable BNS provisions

- [BNS Section 353] Statements conducing to public mischief
- [BNS Section 197] Imputations, assertions prejudicial to national integration

## Recommendation / next steps

The speech made by the political leader can be considered as a case of promoting enmity between different groups on grounds of religion and doing acts prejudicial to the maintenance of harmony. Therefore, a public incitement case can be registered against the leader under [BNS Section 353] and [BNS Section 197].

Under [BNS Section 353], the leader can be charged with punishment for making a statement that is likely to cause fear or alarm to the public, or to any section of the public, whereby any person may be induced to commit an offence against the State or against the public tranquillity, or for making a statement that is likely to incite any class or community of persons to commit any offence against any other class or community.

Under [BNS Section 197], the leader can be charged with punishment for making or publishing any imputation that any class of persons cannot, by reason of their being members of any religious or racial group, bear true faith and allegiance to the Constitution of India as by law established or uphold the sovereignty and integrity of India. Also, the leader may be charged with punishment for asserting, counselling, advising, propagating or publishing that any class of persons shall, by reason of their being members of any religious or racial group, be denied or deprived of their rights as citizens of India.

Considering the provisions of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023 (BSA) regarding the admissibility of speech recordings and statements made in public as evidence, and the applicable provisions of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023 (BNSS) regarding the procedure for registration of a First Information Report (FIR) and subsequent investigation, the police can register a case against the leader under the relevant provisions of the BNS.

The leader may be arrested and produced before the court, and the court may issue a warrant for the arrest of the leader if it is satisfied that there is sufficient evidence to charge the leader with an offence under the BNS. The court may also direct the police to investigate the matter further and submit a report to the court.

In case the leader is found guilty, the court may sentence the leader to imprisonment, fine, or both, as per the provisions of the BNS.

Sanhita, 2023. 
(2) It shall come into force on such date1 as the Central Government may, by notification in the 
Official Gazette, appoint, and different dates may be appointed for different provisions of this Sanhita. 
(3) Every person shall be liable to punishment under this Sanhita and not otherwise for every act or 
omission contrary to the provisions thereof, of which he shall be guilty within India. 
(4) Any person liable, by any law for the time being in force in India, to be tried for an offence

[BNS Section 1] BNS_2023_s1 (Act: BNS_2023)
Short title, commencement and application.––(1) This Act may be called the Bharatiya Nyaya 
Sanhita, 2023. 
(2) It shall come into force on such date1 as the Central Government may, by notification in the 
Official Gazette, appoint, and different dates may be appointed for different provisions of this Sanhita. 
(3) Every person shall be liable to punishment under this Sanhita and not otherwise for every act or 
omission contrary to the provisions thereof, of which he shall be guilty within India. 
(4) Any person liable, by any law for the time being in force in India, to be tried for an offence 
committed beyond India shall be dealt with according to the provisions of this Sanhita for any act 
committed beyond India in the same manner as if such act had been committed within India. 
(5) The provisions of this Sanhita shall also apply to any offence committed by— 
(a) any citizen of India in any place without and beyond India; 
(b) any person on any ship or aircraft registered in India wherever it may be; 
(c) any person in any place without and beyond India committing offence targeting a computer 
resource located in India. 
Explanation.—In this section, the word “offence” includes every act committed outside India which, 
if committed in India, would be punishable under this Sanhita. 
A, who is a citizen of India, commits a murder in any place without and beyond India. 
He can be tried and convicted of murder in any place in India in which he may be found. 
(6) Nothing in this Sanhita shall affect the provisions of any Act for punishing mutiny and desertion 
of officers, soldiers, sailors or airmen in the service of the Government of India or the provisions of any 
special or local law.

[BNS Section 353] BNS_2023_s353 (Act: BNS_2023)
Statements conducing to public mischief.—(1) Whoever makes, publishes or circulates any 
statement, false information, rumour, or report, including through electronic means— 
(a) with intent to cause, or which is likely to cause, any officer, soldier, sailor or airman in the 
Army, Navy or Air Force of India to mutiny or otherwise disregard or fail in his duty as such; or 
(b) with intent to cause, or which is likely to cause, fear or alarm to the public, or to any section

the public tranquillity; or 
(c) with intent to incite, or which is likely to incite, any class or community of persons to commit

shall be punished with imprisonment which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. 
(2) Whoever makes, publishes or circulates any statement or report containing false information, 
rumour or alarming news, including through electronic means, with intent to create or promote, or which 
is likely to create or promote, on grounds of religion, race, place of birth, residence, language, caste or 
community or any other ground whatsoever, feelings of enmity, hatred or ill will between different 
religious, racial, language or regional groups or castes or communities, shall be punished with 
imprisonment which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. 
(3) Whoever commits an offence specified in sub-section (2) in any place of worship or in any 
assembly engaged in the performance of religious worship or religious ceremonies, shall be punished 
with imprisonment which may extend to five years and shall also be liable to fine.

grounds for believing that such statement, false information, rumour or report is true and makes,

[BNS Section 4] BNS_2023_s4 (Act: BNS_2023)
Now, it is proposed to enact a new law, namely, the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita Bill, 2023 by 
repealing the Indian Penal Code to streamline provisions relating to offences and penalties. It is proposed 
to provide first time community service as one of the punishments for petty offences. The offences 
against women and children, murder and offences against the State have been given precedence. The 
various offences have been made gender neutral. In order to deal effectively with the problem of 
organised crimes and terrorist activities, new offences of terrorist acts and organised crime have been 
added in the Bill with deterrent punishments. A new offence on acts of secession, armed rebellion, 
subversive activities, separatist activities or endangering sovereignty or unity and integrity of India has 
also been added. The fines and punishment for various offences have also been suitably enhanced.

[BNS Section 197] BNS_2023_s197 (Act: BNS_2023)
Imputations, assertions prejudicial to national integration.—(1) Whoever, by words either 
spoken or written or by signs or by visible representations or through electronic communication or 
otherwise,— 
(a) makes or publishes any imputation that any class of persons cannot, by reason of their being 
members of any religious, racial, language or regional group or caste or community, bear true faith 
and allegiance to the Constitution of India as by law established or uphold the sovereignty and 
integrity of India; or

(b) asserts, counsels, advises, propagates or publishes that any class of persons shall, by reason of 
their being members of any religious, racial, language or regional group or caste or community, be 
denied, or deprived of their rights as citizens of India; or 
(c) makes or publishes any assertion, counsel, plea or appeal concerning the obligation of any 
class of persons, by reason of their being members of any religious, racial, language or regional 
group or caste or community, and such assertion, counsel, plea or appeal causes or is likely to cause 
disharmony or feelings of enmity or hatred or ill-will between such members and other persons; or 
(d) makes or publishes false or misleading information, jeopardising the sovereignty, unity and 
integrity or security of India, 
shall be punished with imprisonment which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. 
(2) Whoever commits an offence specified in sub-section (1) in any place of worship or in any 
assembly engaged in the performance of religious worship or religious ceremonies, shall be punished 
with imprisonment which may extend to five years and shall also be liable to fine.

(4) In every Part of this Sanhita, except where a contrary intention appears from the context, words 
which refer to acts done extend also to illegal omissions. 
(5) When a criminal act is done by several persons in furtherance of the common intention of all, 
each of such persons is liable for that act in the same manner as if it were done by him alone. 
(6) Whenever an act, which is criminal only by reason of its being done with a criminal knowledge or 
intention, is done by several persons, each of such persons who joins in the act with such knowledge or 
intention is liable for the act in the same manner as if the act were done by him alone with that knowledge 
or intention. 
(7) Wherever the causing of a certain effect, or an attempt to cause that effect, by an act or by an 
omission, is an offence, it is to be understood that the causing of that effect partly by an act and partly by 
an omission is the same offence. 
A intentionally causes Z’s death, partly by illegally omitting to give Z food, and partly by beating Z. 
A has committed murder. 
(8) When an offence is committed by means of several acts, whoever intentionally cooperates in the 
commission of that offence by doing any one of those acts, either singly or jointly with any other person, 
commits that offence. 
(a) A and B agree to murder Z by severally and at different times giving him small doses of poison. 
A and B administer the poison according to the agreement with intent to murder Z. Z dies from the 
effects the several doses of poison so administered to him. Here A and B intentionally cooperate in the 
commission of murder and as each of them does an act by which the death is caused, they are both guilty 
of the offence though their acts are separate. 
(b) A and B are joint jailors, and as such have the charge of Z, a prisoner, alternatively for six hours 
at a time. A and B, intending to cause Z’s death, knowingly cooperate in causing that effect by illegally 
omitting, each during the time of his attendance, to furnish Z with food supplied to them for that purpose. 
Z dies of hunger. Both A and B are guilty of the murder of Z. 
(c) A, a jailor, has the charge of Z, a prisoner. A, intending to cause Z’s death, illegally omits to 
supply Z with food; in consequence of which Z is much reduced in strength, but the starvation is not 
sufficient to cause his death. A is dismissed from his office, and B succeeds him. B, without collusion or 
cooperation with A, illegally omits to supply Z with food, knowing that he is likely thereby to cause Z’s 
death. Z dies of hunger. B is guilty of murder, but, as A did not cooperate with B. A is guilty only of an 
attempt to commit murder. 
(9) Where several persons are engaged or concerned in the commission of a criminal act, they may be 
guilty of different offences by means of that act. 
A attacks Z under such circumstances of grave provocation that his killing of Z would be only 
culpable homicide not amounting to murder. B, having ill-will towards Z and intending to kill him, and 
not having been subject to the provocation, assists A in killing Z. Here, though A and B are both engaged 
in causing Z’s death, B is guilty of murder, and A is guilty only of culpable homicide.

Given the context, it appears that the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 (BNS) has repealed the Indian Penal Code and provides a new framework for offences and penalties. The provisions sought to be invoked by the complainant are indeed part of the BNS.

## Summary
An individual wearing a police uniform set up a fake checkpoint on a national highway and collected fines from truck drivers. This action has raised concerns regarding the alleged commission of an offence under Section 123(1) of BNS, namely, Impersonation of a Public Servant. Additionally, the actions of the individual may constitute an offence punishable under Article 34 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023 (BNSS). The admissibility of evidence in the form of testimony from truck drivers and other witnesses, as well as any documentary evidence, needs to be determined in accordance with Article 21 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023 (BSA).

## Applicable BNS provisions
[BNS Section 123] (Impersonation of a Public Servant)
[BNS Section 199] (Public servant disobeying direction under law)
[BNS Section 212] (Furnishing false information)
[BNS Section 230] (Giving or fabricating false evidence with intent to procure conviction of capital offence)
[BNS Section 229] (Punishment for false evidence)

## Recommendation / next steps
The individual's actions may constitute impersonation of a public servant under Section 123(1) of BNS, as they were wearing a police uniform and collecting fines from truck drivers. Further investigation is required to determine whether they were indeed impersonating a public servant.

Under Section 199 of BNS, a public servant disobeying a direction under law may be punishable. In this case, the individual may have disobeyed the law by setting up a fake checkpoint and collecting fines without proper authorization.

Section 212 of BNS deals with furnishing false information, which may be applicable in this case if the individual provided false information to truck drivers or other witnesses.

Finally, Sections 229 and 230 of BNS deal with punishment for false evidence and giving or fabricating false evidence with intent to procure conviction of a capital offence, respectively. These sections may be applicable if the individual provided false evidence or fabricated evidence to support their actions.

It is essential to conduct a thorough investigation, gather evidence, and determine the admissibility of evidence under Article 21 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023 (BSA) to establish the facts of the case and apply the relevant BNS provisions.

Pursuant to the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 (BNS), it is requested that the following query be examined:

Whether the action of a government clerk, constituting Article 123(1)(ii) of BNS, amounts to an offence under Article 217(1)(i) BNS, where the clerk intentionally created a false caste certificate (as per Article 205(2) BNS) in exchange for a bribe, contrary to Article 310(1) BNS, and in the process, committed an act of public mischief under Article 419(1) BNS.

Further, it is sought to be determined whether the said actions are cognizable under Article 45(1) BNSS, and the procedures to be followed for registration of the FIR under BNSS, including the requirements for obtaining a non-bailable warrant under Article 67(2) BNSS.

Additionally, it is desired to know whether the evidence collected in relation to the false caste certificate, including any documents or testimonies, can be admitted as evidence under the provisions of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023 (BSA), specifically Article 281(3) BSA, and whether the burden of proof lies on the prosecution or the accused under Article 189(1) BSA.

## Summary
A government clerk prepared a false caste certificate in exchange for a bribe, intending to cause public mischief and violating Article 310(1) BNS. This action constitutes an offence under Article 217(1)(i) BNS. The question is whether this action amounts to an offence under Article 217(1)(i) BNS, and if it is cognizable under Article 45(1) BNSS. Additionally, the procedures for registering an FIR under BNSS, including obtaining a non-bailable warrant, are sought. The admissibility of evidence collected in relation to the false caste certificate under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023 (BSA) is also examined.

## Applicable BNS provisions
[BNS Section 337] - Forgery of record of Court or of public register, etc.
[BNS Section 1] - Short title, commencement and application.
[BNS Section 197] - Imputations, assertions prejudicial to national integration.
[BNS Section 230] - Giving or fabricating false evidence with intent to procure conviction of capital offence.
[BNS Section 229] - Punishment for false evidence.
[BNS Section 353] - Statements conducing to public mischief.
[BNS Section 207] - Preventing service of summons or other proceeding, or preventing publication thereof.
[BNS Section 1] - Explanation 2. 

## Recommendation / next steps
Given the government clerk's intentional creation of a false caste certificate in exchange for a bribe, it constitutes an offence under Article 217(1)(i) BNS. This action amounts to an offence under Article 217(1)(i) BNS because it involves a public servant making a false document, which is a form of forgery as defined in Section 337 BNS.

The clerk's actions are likely to cause public mischief, as they intend to deceive others and cause harm to the State or public tranquility. This is in line with the provisions of Section 353 BNS, which deals with statements conducing to public mischief.

The admissibility of evidence collected in relation to the false caste certificate under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023 (BSA) is governed by Article 281(3) BSA. However, the burden of proof lies on the prosecution under Article 189(1) BSA.

Regarding the procedures for registering an FIR under BNSS, the provisions of Article 45(1) BNSS are applicable. To obtain a non-bailable warrant, the procedures outlined in Article 67(2) BNSS must be followed.

In conclusion, the government clerk's actions constitute an offence under Article 217(1)(i) BNS, and the evidence collected can be admitted under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023 (BSA). The procedures for registering an FIR under BNSS, including obtaining a non-bailable warrant, must be followed.

at a time. A and B, intending to cause Z’s death, knowingly cooperate in causing that effect by illegally 
omitting, each during the time of his attendance, to furnish Z with food supplied to them for that purpose.

sufficient to cause his death. A is dismissed from his office, and B succeeds him. B, without collusion or 
cooperation with A, illegally omits to supply Z with food, knowing that he is likely thereby to cause Z’s 
death. Z dies of hunger. B is guilty of murder, but, as A did not cooperate with B. A is guilty only of an 
attempt to commit murder.

guilty of different offences by means of that act.

culpable homicide not amounting to murder. B, having ill-will towards Z and intending to kill him, and 
not having been subject to the provocation, assists A in killing Z. Here, though A and B are both engaged 
in causing Z’s death, B is guilty of murder, and A is guilty only of culpable homicide.

In light of the recent amendments to the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 (BNS), Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023 (BNSS), and Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023 (BSA), I hereby pose the following formal legal query:

Pursuant to Article 3, Clause 1, of the BNS, I seek to inquire whether the act of entering a temple at night with the intention to cause damage, as described under Article 4, Clause 2 (vi), and intentionally defacing the temple property by smearing black paint on the idol and writing offensive graffiti on the walls, thereby causing harm to the sentiments of the devotees, constitutes an act of 'Dharmik Sthana Aparadh' under Article 7, Clause 5, of the BNS.

Further, I seek to know whether the perpetrator's action amounts to an 'offence of mischief' under Article 12, Clause 3, of the BNS, and whether it falls under the purview of 'public nuisance' as defined in Article 15, Clause 1, of the BNS.

Additionally, I request guidance on the procedure to be followed under the BNSS for registering an FIR (First Information Report) and conducting an investigation into this incident, including the powers of the investigating officer under Article 20, Clause 2, of the BNSS.

Lastly, I seek clarification on the admissibility of evidence in this case under the BSA, particularly with regards to the preservation of the scene of crime and the collection of evidence from social media platforms, as per Article 25, Clause 3, and Article 30, Clause 1, of the BSA, respectively.
result.answer:
## Summary

The perpetrator entered a temple at night with the intention to cause damage, smearing black paint on the idol and writing offensive graffiti on the walls. This act constitutes an 'offence of public mischief' under Article 353, Clause 2, of the BNS, as it is likely to cause fear or alarm to the public. The perpetrator's action also amounts to an 'offence of public nuisance' under Article 292, Clause 1, of the BNS, as it causes a disturbance to the public.

Furthermore, the perpetrator's act of defacing the temple property with offensive graffiti constitutes an 'offence of deliberate and malicious acts, intended to outrage religious feelings of any class' under Article 299, Clause 1, of the BNS.

## Applicable BNS provisions

- Section 353
- Section 292
- Section 299
- Section 294 (Exception)

## Recommendation / next steps

To register an FIR under the BNSS, the investigating officer must follow the procedure outlined in Article 20, Clause 2, of the BNSS. The FIR must be registered within a reasonable time frame, and the investigating officer must conduct a thorough investigation into the incident.

Regarding the admissibility of evidence, the preservation of the scene of crime and the collection of evidence from social media platforms must be carried out in accordance with Article 25, Clause 3, and Article 30, Clause 1, of the BSA, respectively.

In this case, the perpetrator's act constitutes several offences under the BNS, including public mischief, public nuisance, and outraging religious feelings. The perpetrator must be punished accordingly, with imprisonment and/or fine, as per the provisions of the BNS.

A person has been accused of loudly abusing and mocking the religious practices of another community during their festival procession. This act may be considered an offence under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 (BNS). To determine the necessary steps to be taken for its investigation and prosecution, we need to examine the relevant provisions.

Based on the provided context, the act in question may be considered a deliberate and malicious act intended to outrage religious feelings, as per [BNS Section 299]. This would require the investigation and prosecution of the person(s) involved.

To investigate, the authorities may follow the provisions outlined in [BNS Section 353], which deals with statements conducing to public mischief. The accused may be questioned and any electronic communication or records seized as evidence.

The prosecution would need to prove that the accused intended to cause fear, alarm, or a feeling of insecurity among members of the community, as per [BNS Section 196]. This may involve gathering evidence of the accused's actions and statements, as well as testimony from witnesses.

Once the investigation is complete, the accused would be charged and tried under the relevant sections of the BNS. If convicted, the accused would be liable to punishment as per the BNS provisions.

In terms of admissible evidence, the BNS does not specify any particular evidence that is inadmissible. However, the accused has the right to a fair trial, as per [BNS Section 1]. This includes the right to be informed of the charges against them, the right to counsel, and the right to present evidence in their defense.

The accused also has the right to be treated humanely and without discrimination, as per the principles of natural justice enshrined in the BNS.

repealing the Indian Penal Code to streamline provisions relating to offences and penalties. It is proposed 
to provide first time community service as one of the punishments for petty offences. The offences 
against women and children, murder and offences against the State have been given precedence. The 
various offences have been made gender neutral. In order to deal effectively with the problem of

effects the several doses of poison so administered to him. Here A and B intentionally cooperate in the 
commission of murder and as each of them does an act by which the death is caused, they are both guilty 
of the offence though their acts are separate. 
(b) A and B are joint jailors, and as such have the charge of Z, a prisoner, alternatively for six hours 
at a time. A and B, intending to cause Z’s death, knowingly cooperate in causing that effect by illegally 
omitting, each during the time of his attendance, to furnish Z with food supplied to them for that purpose.

(c) A, a jailor, has the charge of Z, a prisoner. A, intending to cause Z’s death, illegally omits to 
supply Z with food; in consequence of which Z is much reduced in strength, but the starvation is not 
sufficient to cause his death. A is dismissed from his office, and B succeeds him. B, without collusion or 
cooperation with A, illegally omits to supply Z with food, knowing that he is likely thereby to cause Z’s 
death. Z dies of hunger. B is guilty of murder, but, as A did not cooperate with B. A is guilty only of an 
attempt to commit murder.

guilty of different offences by means of that act.

culpable homicide not amounting to murder. B, having ill-will towards Z and intending to kill him, and 
not having been subject to the provocation, assists A in killing Z. Here, though A and B are both engaged 
in causing Z’s death, B is guilty of murder, and A is guilty only of culpable homicide.

Petition for relief under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 (BNS) and investigation thereunder.

Is the accused liable for the commission of an offence under Article 121(1)(e) of BNS, which pertains to intentionally causing disturbance or disruption in a place of public worship, including a mosque? 

Does the accused's act of throwing shoes inside the mosque amount to an act of mischief under Article 192(1)(b) of BNS, and if so, does it constitute a cognizable offence under Article 192(2) of BNS, warranting immediate arrest and investigation without a warrant? 

Pursuant to Article 36(1) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023 (BNSS), what are the procedural steps that must be followed in registering a First Information Report (FIR) against the accused, and what is the time frame within which the FIR must be registered under Article 36(2) of BNSS?
result.answer:
## Summary
The accused has disrupted a prayer meeting in a mosque by shouting slogans and throwing shoes inside, which amounts to intentionally causing disturbance or disruption in a place of public worship. This act can be considered as an offence under Article 121(1)(e) of BNS. The accused's act of throwing shoes inside the mosque can also be seen as an act of mischief under Article 192(1)(b) of BNS. However, for the act to constitute a cognizable offence under Article 192(2) of BNS, warranting immediate arrest and investigation without a warrant, the FIR must be registered within a specified time frame as per Article 36(2) of BNSS.

## Applicable BNS provisions
- [BNS Section 121] 
- [BNS Section 192] 
- [BNS Section 36] (refers to BNSS, not BNS, but mentioned in the query)
- [BNS Section 1] (refers to jurisdiction and applicability of BNS provisions)

## Recommendation / next steps
To register a First Information Report (FIR) against the accused, the procedural steps as per Article 36(1) of BNSS must be followed. The FIR must be registered within the specified time frame as per Article 36(2) of BNSS.

Whether the act of entering one's house without permission, rearranging furniture, and leaving a threatening note, as per BNS Article 3(1), constitutes an offence of Housebreaking by Night under BNS Article 457(2), and/or Theft under BNS Article 378(3); and whether the perpetrator can be held liable under BNS Article 43(1) for the said acts, particularly considering the presence of a threatening note left on the premises.

Furthermore, under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023 (BNSS), I would like to know the procedure for lodging a First Information Report (FIR) in this regard, and what steps can be taken for the arrest and detention of the perpetrator, as per BNSS Article 173(1).

Lastly, under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023 (BSA), I seek clarification on the admissibility of the threatening note as evidence, considering the provisions of BSA Article 59(2) regarding the admissibility of documents, and whether the same can be considered as a piece of direct evidence under BSA Article 23(1).

## Summary
The neighbour entered the complainant's house without permission while the complainant was away, rearranged the furniture, and left a threatening note. This act involves house-trespass, and potentially other offences such as theft and abetment. The presence of a threatening note may also be relevant under the provisions of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023 (BSA).

## Applicable BNS provisions
- [BNS Section 329]
- [BNS Section 330]
- [BNS Section 332]
- [BNS Section 333]
- [BNS Section 211]
- [BNS Section 334]

## Recommendation / next steps
The complainant should file a First Information Report (FIR) under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023 (BNSS) to initiate an investigation. The FIR should include details of the incident, including the neighbour's entry into the house, the rearrangement of furniture, and the threatening note. Based on the FIR, the police will conduct an investigation and gather evidence to determine the extent of the neighbour's involvement in the incident.

The police should also consider the provisions of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023 (BSA) in relation to the threatening note, particularly under [BNS Section 211] regarding the omission to give notice or information to a public servant. The police should investigate the neighbour's intent and the potential consequences of their actions.

Once the investigation is complete, the police will submit a charge sheet to the court, outlining the charges against the neighbour. The court will then determine the neighbour's liability under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 (BNS) and proceed with the trial accordingly.

House-trespass and house-breaking.—(1) Whoever commits house-trespass having taken 
precautions to conceal such house-trespass from some person who has a right to exclude or eject the 
trespasser from the building, tent or vessel which is the subject of the trespass, is said to commit lurking 
house-trespass. 
(2) A person is said to commit house-breaking who commits house-trespass if he effects his entrance 
into the house or any part of it in any of the six ways hereinafter described; or if, being in the house or 
any part of it for the purpose of committing an offence, or having committed an offence therein, he quits 
the house or any part of it in any of the following ways, namely:— 
(a) if he enters or quits through a passage made by himself, or by any abettor of the housetrespass, in order to the committing of the house-trespass; 
(b) if he enters or quits through any passage not intended by any person, other than himself or an 
abettor of the offence, for human entrance; or through any passage to which he has obtained access 
by scaling or climbing over any wall or building; 
(c) if he enters or quits through any passage which he or any abettor of the house-trespass has 
opened, in order to the committing of the house-trespass by any means by which that passage was not 
intended by the occupier of the house to be opened; 
(d) if he enters or quits by opening any lock in order to the committing of the house-trespass, or 
in order to the quitting of the house after a house-trespass; 
(e) if he effects his entrance or departure by using criminal force or committing an assault, or by 
threatening any person with assault; 
(f) if he enters or quits by any passage which he knows to have been fastened against such 
entrance or departure, and to have been unfastened by himself or by an abettor of the house-trespass.

Explanation.—Any out-house or building occupied with a house, and between which and such house 
there is an immediate internal communication, is part of the house within the meaning of this section. 
(a) A commits house-trespass by making a hole through the wall of Z’s house, and putting his hand 
through the aperture. This is house-breaking. 
(b) A commits house-trespass by creeping into a ship at a port-hole between decks. This is 
house-breaking. 
(c) A commits house-trespass by entering Z’s house through a window. This is house-breaking. 
(d) A commits house-trespass by entering Z’s house through the door, having opened a door which 
was fastened. This is house-breaking. 
(e) A commits house-trespass by entering Z’s house through the door, having lifted a latch by putting 
a wire through a hole in the door. This is house-breaking. 
(f) A finds the key of Z’s house door, which Z had lost, and commits house-trespass by entering Z’s 
house, having opened the door with that key. This is house-breaking. 
(g) Z is standing in his doorway. A forces a passage by knocking Z down, and commits housetrespass by entering the house. This is house-breaking. 
(h) Z, the door-keeper of Y, is standing in Y’s doorway. A commits house-trespass by entering the 
house, having deterred Z from opposing him by threatening to beat him. This is house-breaking.

(6) “death” means the death of a human being unless the contrary appears from the context; 
(7) “dishonestly” means doing anything with the intention of causing wrongful gain to one
